# Chapter 1: ENTITY AND FINANCIAL STATEMENTS 

## 1.1 ENTITY AND FINANCIAL STATEMENTS

$\Rightarrow$ Any entity whether business oriented or not conducts various transactions which in one way or other involve monetary or related transactions. The entity has to keep records for each and every transaction in an appropriate manner so that any future conflict or confusion about these transactions could be avoided and the transactions could be presented fairly and transparently as per the need.
$\Rightarrow$ The act of keeping records for all the transactions is referred as book-keeping. The entity has to follow various laws of book keeping and reporting framework in order to present the transactions appropriately. Book-keeping is the recording, on a day-to-day basis of the financial transactions and information pertaining to a business. It is concerned with ensuring that records of those individual financial transactions are accurate, up-to-date and comprehensive.
$\Rightarrow$ Book-keeping provides the information from which accounts are prepared but is a distinct process, preliminary to accounting. Each transaction, whether it is a question of purchase or sale, or change of loans, has to be recorded in the books.
$\Rightarrow$ The results of these transactions are evaluated at each identified period known as Financial Year.
$\Rightarrow$ In Nepal, Financial Year (hereinafter referred as FY) starts from $1^{\text {st }}$ of Shrawan and Ends on End of Asar of following year. However, It is not necessary that FY must be of 12 months. Shorter period may be justified as per the incorporation of the company or dissolution of the company.
$\Rightarrow$ The results of transactions are reflected via Financial Statements of the entity. If the financial statements contain errors or misstatements, it becomes difficult to analyze the situation of business thus; it becomes difficult to make appropriate decisions.

## 1.2 FINANCIAL STATEMENT

$\Rightarrow$ As per Nepal Accounting Standards-01 on Presentation of Financial Statements, a complete set of Financial Statements consist of the following:

| Statements | Purpose |
| :-- | :-- |
| 1. Balance Sheet | Shows the position of Assets, Liabilities \& Equity as on the <br> date. |
| 2. Profit \& Loss A/c | Shows the results of operation during the FY i.e Profit or <br> Loss/ Income \& Expenses ( It is also known as Statement of <br> Performance) |
| 3. Cash Flow Statement | Shows the movements of funds during FY i.e Inflows and <br> Outflows |
| 4. Statement of Change in Equity | It shows the change in position of Equity for comparable <br> periods. |

---

| 5. Comparatives | It reflects the restatement or reclassification of Financial Information  |
| --- | --- |
|  6. Notes to Accounts | Explain the various adjustments and important matters related to Financial Statements ( They are also known as Explanatory Notes)  |

## 1.3 USERS OF FINANCIAL STATEMENTS

|  Users | Purpose  |
| --- | --- |
|  1. Management | To evaluate the Performance of the entity for decision making  |
|  2. Shareholders / Owners | To know the results of their investments and understand the position of business.  |
|  3. Employees | To identify the criteria for bonus, wages and other employee benefits  |
|  4. Government | To collect taxes (revenue to government) and keep track records of the entity.  |
|  5. Suppliers | To determine the credit worthiness of the company (i.e. whether to supply the goods on credit or not)  |
|  6. Customers | To Know about the performance and quality of the business (general viability)  |
|  7. Prospective Investors | To determine whether or not to invest in the business.  |

## 1.4 RESPONSIBILITY OF FINANCIAL STATEMENT

It is the responsibility of management

- To maintain an up-to-date and proper accounting system in order to prepare financial statements.
- To select and implement appropriate accounting policies and standards.
- To design and implement suitable Internal Control System.
- To prevent, correct and detect the misstatements on timely basis.

## 1.5 MEANING OF AUDIT

- The term audit is derived from the Latin term 'Audire,' which means to hear. In earlier days, an auditor used to listen to the accounts read over by an accountant in order to check them.
- In the converse manner the Auditor reports the status of Financial Statements to the users of Financial Statements through his Audit Report thereby meaning that the users hear the status of Financial Statements through Auditor.
- An Audit is an Independent Examination of Financial Information of any entity, whether profit oriented or not, and irrespective of its size or legal form, with a view to express an opinion thereon. (Definition of ICAI)
- As per the definition of Prof. L.R. Dicksee, "Auditing is an examination of accounting records undertaken with a view to establish whether they correctly and completely reflect the transactions to which they relate".
- As per the definition of R.K Mautz, "Auditing is being concerned with the verification of accounting records."
- As per the definition of R.K Mautz, "Auditing is being concerned with the verification of  accounting data with deterring the accuracy and reliability of accounting statements and reports."
- Audit Act 2048 defines audit as "Examination of the accounts and analysis and evaluation made on the basis thereof."
- Once the Financial Statements are prepared by the management, it is necessary to check whether or not such statements fairly reflect the position of the entity. It is therefore, independent examination of financial statements is done by a professionally qualified person. The process of such examination is referred as "Audit" and the person conducting Audit is known as "Auditor".

## 1.6 HISTORY OF AUDIT 

$\Rightarrow$ The concept of Audit can be traced back to ancient countries such as Mesopotamia, Greece, Egypt, Rome, U.K. and India. Even the Vedas contain reference to accounting and Auditing.
$\Rightarrow$ Mesopotamian relics of commercial transactions relating to period $3600-3200 \mathrm{BC}$ also reveal tiny marks, dots and ticks at the side of the figures which indicate that such figures were examined later.
$\Rightarrow$ As mentioned in the book "Contemporary Auditing" by CA. Kamal Gupta, The system of accounting and auditing of state revenue and expenditure become sophisticated under the Maurya and Hindu kings in ancient Indian era.
$\Rightarrow$ In Europe, the region of UK, the establishment of the exchequer is attributed to reign of Henry I (1100-1135 AD). The Exchequer's account reveals that there was a regular system of accounting and auditing of state transactions in the $12^{\text {th }}$ century.

## 1.9 AUDITOR 

$\Rightarrow$ The professionally qualified person who conducts the Audit is known as Auditor. Professional Qualification means licensed by a professional body (in context of Nepal, ICAN has the authority to issue the license) in order to be eligible to conduct audit of financial statements.
$\Rightarrow$ The following criteria are considered for eligibility to act as an Auditor:
a. The person is member of ICAN.
i. He must have passed final/ membership exams conducted by ICAN. OR
ii. He is recognized as member of ICAN ( Registered Auditor)
b. He must hold Certificate of Practice (COP).
c. He must not be disqualified under any other provisions of Relevant Acts.

In Nepal, the members of ICAN (eligible to act as auditor) are classified as follows :

| Members | Class |
| :-- | :-- |
| Chartered Accountants/ Fellow Chartered Accountants | A |
| Registered Auditors | B,C,D |

---

### Qualities of an Auditor:
The auditor must possess following qualities:

a. Integrity and
Auditor must be sincere and honest while discharging his duties as an auditor.
Auditor must work with an unbiased approach.
Auditor should not be influenced by any factors and should
express the opinion independently.

c. Knowledge
Auditor should have sufficient knowledge of Laws, Acts, Regulations, and Standards etc. that are required for conducting the audit.
He should be well informed about the clients business too.

d. Communication Skills
Since the auditor has to enquire and discuss various matters during the course of audit, he requires good communication skills in order to communicate with various personnel(s) within the entity.

e. Judgment and
Auditor has to deal with management staffs as well his own staffs, therefore he should have good judgement about the situations to deal with.
He should also apply judgment in selecting the transactions for checking.

f. Logical and Technical
Auditor should be updated with latest laws and regulations. Skills
He should possess good logical skills to analyse and interpret the problem.

g. Confidentiality
Auditor should not disclose information of the client obtained during the course of the audit unless:
	a. Permitted by the client $O R$
	b. Required by law

### Functions of Auditor

The following are considered as the function of the auditor.
Alternatively referred as basic aspects to be covered by auditor.
a. Examination of :
	$\checkmark$ Accounting system and internal controls to ensure their correctness.
	$\checkmark$ Books of accounts to ensure their arithmetical accuracy.
	$\checkmark$ Documentary Evidences to support books of accounts.
	$\checkmark$ Appropriateness of recording and accounting policies
b. Verification of Assets and Liabilities
c. Ensuring compliance with relevant laws and regulations.
d. Checking whether or not financial statements give a True and Fair view.

## 1.10 INDEPENDENCE OF AUDITORS

Independence means the state of free will where the judgment of the person is not affected by any factors such as interest or influence.
$\Rightarrow$ Auditor independence refers to the independence of the external auditor. It is characterized by integrity and an objective approach to the audit process. The concept requires the auditor to carry out his or her work freely and in an objective manner.

---

- Simply, An auditor is required to report on the status of financial statements prepared by the management of the entity and his report is trusted by the users of financial statements. Therefore auditor should report in an unbiased manner i.e. independently without any interest or influence.
- As per section 290.6 of the Code of Ethics 2015 recommended by ICAN, Independence comprises:
a. Independence of Mind (no any emotional relation)
It refers to the state of mind that permits the expression of a conclusion without being affected by influences that compromise professional judgment, thereby allowing an individual to act with integrity and exercise objectivity and professional skepticism.
b. Independence in Appearance (no any family or business relation visible)

The avoidance of facts and circumstances that are so significant that a reasonable and informed third party would be likely to conclude, weighing all the specific facts and circumstances, that a firm's, or a member of the audit team's, integrity, objectivity or professional skepticism has been compromised.
Simply, Independence in appearance is what third parties would perceive as being independent. (i.e third party's point of view regarding auditors independence).
For Eq. If Mr. $R$ is appointed as an auditor of STP Ltd and.Mr. U, uncle of Mr. R is working there as Finance Director, then the users (third parties) may consider that Mr. R is not independent as he may be biased.

- The International Federation of Accountants (IFAC) provides a framework of principles that members of assurance teams, firms and network firms should use to identify threats to independence, evaluate the significance of those threats, and, if the threats are other than clearly insignificant, identify and apply safeguards to eliminate the threats or reduce them to an acceptable level, such that independence of mind and independence in appearance are not compromised.
- In situations when no safeguards are available to reduce the threat to an acceptable level, the only possible actions are to eliminate the activities or interest creating the threat, or to refuse to accept or continue the assurance engagement.


### Threats to Independence 

| Threats | Explanation |
| :--: | :--: |
| 1. Self-interest threat | It occurs when the audit firm or a member of the audit team could benefit from a financial interest in, or other self-interest conflict with, an audit client. <br> Examples: <br> $\checkmark$ A direct financial interest or material indirect financial interest in an audit client; <br> $\checkmark$ A loan or guarantee to or from an audit client or any of its directors or officers; <br> $\checkmark$ Undue dependence on total fees from an audit client; Concern about the possibility of losing the engagement; fees overdue for long period; <br> $\checkmark$ Having a close business relationship with an audit client; <br> $\checkmark$ Potential employment with an audit client; and <br> $\checkmark$ Contingent fees relating to audit engagements. |

---

|    2. Self-review threat     |                                                            It occurs when the audit firm, or an individual audit team member is put in a position of reviewing subject matter for which the firm or individual was previously responsible, and which is significant in the context of the audit engagement. <br> Examples: <br> $\checkmark$ A member of the audit team being, or having recently been, a director, officer or other employee of the audit client in a position to exert direct and significant influence over the subject matter of the audit engagement. <br> $\checkmark$ Performing services for an audit client that directly affect the subject matter of the current, or a subsequent, audit engagement; and <br> $\checkmark$ Preparation of original data used to generate financial statements or preparation of other records that are the subject matter of the audit engagement.                                                             |
| :--------------------------: | :-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------: |
|      3. Advocacy threat      |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            It occurs when the audit firm, or a member of the audit team, promotes, or may be perceived to promote, an audit client's position or opinion to the point where objectivity may be compromised. Examples: <br> $\checkmark$ Dealing in, or being a promoter of, shares or other securities in an audit client; and <br> $\checkmark$ Acting as an advocate on behalf of an audit client in litigation or in resolving disputes with third parties.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|    4. Familiarity threat     | It occurs when, by virtue of a close relationship with an audit client, its directors, officers or employees, an audit firm or a member of the audit team becomes too sympathetic to the client's interests. Examples: <br> $\checkmark$ A Member of the audit team having a close family member who, as a director, officer or other employee of the audit client, is in a position to exert direct and significant influence over the subject matter of the audit engagement; <br> $\checkmark$ A former partner of the firm being a director, officer or other employee of the audit client, in a position to exert direct and significant influence over the subject matter of the audit engagement; <br> $\checkmark$ Long association of a senior member of the audit team with the audit client; and <br> $\checkmark$ Acceptance of gifts or hospitality, unless the value is clearly insignificant, from the audit client, its directors, officers or employees. |
| 5. (intimidation threat fear |                                                                                                                                                                                            It occurs when a member of the audit team may be deterred from acting objectively and exercising professional skepticism by threats, actual or perceived, from the directors, officers or employees of a client. <br> Examples: <br> $\checkmark$ Threat of replacement over a disagreement with the application of an accounting principle; <br> $\checkmark$ Pressure to reduce inappropriately the extent of work performed in order to reduce fees; and <br> $\checkmark$ Dominant personality in a senior position at the audit client, controlling dealings with the auditor                                                                                                                                                                                             |

---

## 1.11 THE SAFEGUARDS TO THREATS 

Since the client itself or the shareholders make the payment to the auditor it is important to recognize that independence can never be absolute. The purpose of safeguards is to reduce the impact of threats to independence to a level that does not impair the auditor's opinion-forming process in fact, or in the perception of a reasonable and informed observer (i.e. Third Party)
$\Rightarrow$ When threats are identified, appropriate safeguards should be identified and applied to eliminate the threats or reduce them to an acceptable level.
$\Rightarrow$ The nature of the safeguards to be applied will vary depending upon the circumstances. Consideration should always be given to what a reasonable third party having knowledge of all relevant information; including safeguards applied, and would conclude to be unacceptable.
$\Rightarrow$ The consideration will be affected by matters such as the significance of the threat, the nature of the audit engagement, the intended users of the audit report and the structure of the firm.
$\Rightarrow$ If acceptable safeguards cannot be applied, the particular engagement should not be undertaken.
$\Rightarrow$ Eliminating or reducing the magnitude of the transaction; or
$\checkmark$ Removing the individual from the audit team.
Safeguards fall in three categories:
a. Created by the profession, legislation or regulation;
b. Within the audit client; and
c. Within the audit firm's own systems and procedures.

| Safeguards | Inclusions |
| :--: | :--: |
| Safeguards created by the profession, legislation or regulation | $\checkmark$ Educational, training and experience requirements for entry into the profession; <br> $\checkmark$ Continuing education requirements; <br> $\checkmark$ Professional standards and monitoring and disciplinary processes; <br> $\checkmark$ External review of an audit firm's quality control system; and <br> $\checkmark$ Legislation governing the independence requirements of the audit firm. |
| Safeguards within the audit client (Auditee) | $\checkmark$ When the audit client's management appoints the firm, persons other than management ratify or approve the appointment; <br> $\checkmark$ The audit client has competent employees to make managerial decisions; <br> $\checkmark$ Policies and procedures that emphasize the audit client's commitment to fair financial reporting; <br> $\checkmark$ Internal procedures that ensure objective choices in commissioning non-audit engagements; and <br> $\checkmark$ A corporate governance structure, such as an audit committee, that provides appropriate oversight and communications regarding the audit firm's services. |
| Safeguards within the audit firm | $\checkmark$ Quality control of audit engagements; |

---
## 1.12 RELATIONSHIP OF AUDITING WITH OTHER DISCIPLINES

| 1.12 RELATIONSHIP OF AUDITING WITH OTHER DISCIPLINES |                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| a. Accounting                                        | $\checkmark$ The financial statements are the results of accounting process.                                                                                                                     |
|                                                      | $\checkmark$ The Auditor examines Financial Statements with an objective of expressing the opinion. Therefore for conducting an audit, expert knowledge of accounting is required.               |
| b. Law                                               | $\checkmark$ NSA 250 requires understanding of applicable laws to the entity and report violation thereof.                                                                                       |
|                                                      | $\checkmark$ Auditor should be well informed about applicable laws to client entity in order to ensure their compliance, for example: Income Tax Laws, VAT Laws, Banking Laws, Company Laws etc. |
| c. Economics                                         | $\checkmark$ Since the accounting records the data relating to economic activities, Auditor should have good knowledge on economics (primarily micro economics) to perform audit efficiently.    |
| d. Behavioral Science                                | $\checkmark$ The auditor has to deal with many people during the course of audit to obtain information relating to audit.                                                                        |
|                                                      | $\checkmark$ He should also direct and supervise his own staff.                                                                                                                                  |
|                                                      | $\checkmark$ Therefore he should have knowledge of human behavior and basic psychology while dealing with the people.                                                                            |
| e. Statistics and Mathematics                        | $\checkmark$ Since the auditing deals with financial figures and amounts, the auditor needs to have good mathematical and statistical skills to verify the accuracy of transaction and amounts.  |

DIFFERENCE BETWEEN AUDITING AND ACCOUNTING

| Basis | Accounting | Auditing |
| :--: | :--: | :--: |
| Meaning | Accounting means systematically keeping the records of the accounts of an organization and preparation of financial statements at the end of the financial year. | Auditingis independent examination of the books of account and financial statements of an organization. |
| Governed By | Accounting Standards (AS's) | Standards on Auditing (SA's) |
| Responsible Person | Accountant (Anyone having good knowledge on Accounting) | Licensed Auditor |
| Purpose | To show the performance, profitability and financial position of an organization. | To reveal the fact, that to which extent financial statement of an organization gives true and fair view |
| Period | Accounting is a continuous process, i.e. day to day recording of transactions are done. | Auditing is a periodic process. |
| Time of Occurrence | Prior to Audit | Auditing starts where accounting ends. |

DIFFERENCE BETWEEN AUDITING AND INVESTIGATION

| Basis | Auditing | Investigation |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| Meaning | The process of examination of <br> financial statements with an <br> objective of expression of opinion <br> thereon. | An Enquiry conducted for <br> establishing a fact and finding the <br> truth. |

| Entity And Financial Statements |  |  |
| :--: | :--: | :--: |
| Nature | General Examination of Books of Accounts/ Financial Statements | In Depth Examination of records. |
| Evidence | Persuasive rather than Conclusive | Decisive(Conclusive) in nature |
| Inherent Limitations | More because of Test Checking | Less because of detailed examination |
| Period | Annually (Generally) | As per requirement |
| Responsible Person | Chartered Accountant Or <br> Registered Auditor | Experts |
| Reporting | General Purpose i.e Users of Financial Statements | Confidential- Only to needful person |
| Approval | Not a Doubtful Approach | Doubtful Approach |

## 1.13 OBJECTIVES OF AUDIT \& ASSURANCE OF FINANCIAL STATEMENTS 

![img-2.jpeg](assets/audit%20book%20ch1_img-2.jpeg)

As per para 3 of NSA 200,
$\checkmark$ The purpose of an audit is to enhance the degree of confidence of intended users in the financial statements. This is achieved by the expression of an opinion by the auditor on whether the financial statements are prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with an applicable financial reporting framework.
$\checkmark$ In the case of most general purpose frameworks, that opinion is on whether the financial statements are presented fairly, in all material respects, or give a true and fair view in accordance with the framework.

---
### Objectives of Audit/ Assurance are divided into two parts:
**A. Primary Objective**
$\Rightarrow$ Primary objective of audit is Expression of opinion of Financial Statements of the Entity.
$\Rightarrow$ The opinion expressed conveys whether or not the Financial Statements give a "True and Fair View"
<u>True and Fair View</u>
The auditor express an opinion that Financial Statements give a True and Fair View when:
Financial Statements are prepared according to applicable FRF.
	$\checkmark$ Financial Statements have complied with all relevant laws and regulations.
	$\checkmark$ The books of accounts are arithmetically correct (i.e Arithmetical Accuracy) 
	$\checkmark$ The transactions are supported by sufficient appropriate evidence.           
	$\checkmark$ The transactions are authorized and approved by competent body.              
	$\checkmark$ The transactions are properly classified as Capital and Revenue.             
	$\checkmark$ The assets and liabilities are neither understated nor overvalued.           
	$\checkmark$ The Financial Statements are free from misstatements.                        
	$\checkmark$ The Financial Statements disclose all relevant facts.                        

**B. Secondary Objective** 
	$\Rightarrow$ Secondary objective of audit is to detect and report the misstatements.  
	$\Rightarrow$ Misstatements may be due to fraud or error in the Financial Statements.  
	$\Rightarrow$ Auditor should always remain alert to the possibility of detection of fraud and error in the financial statements. Without ensuring that financial statements are free from misstatements, the auditor cannot give an opinion on "True and Fair" view of the financial statements.  
**As per NSA 240, Para 4 \& 5,**  
	$\checkmark$ The primary responsibility for the prevention and detection of fraud rests with both those charged with governance of the entity and management.  
	$\checkmark$ An auditor conducting an audit in accordance with NSAs is responsible for obtaining reasonable assurance that the financisl statements taken as a whole are free from material misstatement, whether caused by fraud or error. 
	 $\Rightarrow$ However, an audit may not disclose all the misstatements in the financial statements due to inherent limitations of Audit. Auditor cannot be held responsible for non-detection if he has conducted audit with due care as per the basic principles governing an audit.  

### Reviewing auditor's performance:

To determine whether or not auditor has followed basic principles governing the audit, the following test is applied: $\checkmark$ Whether the auditor has exercised reasonable care and skill in carrying out his work $\checkmark$ Whether the errors and frauds were such that they could have been detected in the ordinary

---

### Entity And Financial Statements 

course of checking without the aid of any special efforts
$\checkmark$ Whether the auditor had any reasons to suspect the existence of frauds or errors and
$\checkmark$ Whether errors or frauds were so deep laid that the same might not have been detected by normal audit procedure.

The case of Kingston Cotton Mills Company, 1896

### AUDITOR IS A WATCHDOG, NOT A BLOODHOUND

Lord Justice Lopez in the Kingston Cotton Mill, 1896, said that the auditor's role in an entity should be that of a 'watchdog' rather than a 'bloodhound'. Lord Justice Lopez said:
$\checkmark$ "It is the duty of an auditor to bring to bear on the work he has to perform that skill, care and caution which a reasonably careful, cautious auditor would use. What is reasonable skill, care and caution must depend on the particular circumstances of each case. An auditor is not bound to be a detective, or, as was said to approach his work with suspicion, or with a foregone conclusion that there is something wrong. He is a watchdog not a bloodhound. He is justified in believing tried servants of the company in whom confidence is placed by the company. He is entitled to assume that they are honest and rely upon their representations, provided he takes reasonable care.
Source: Lord Justice Lopez - Kingston Cotton Mill 1896.
$\checkmark$ The view here was that the auditor should act with such reasonable care and skill in order that their work will have a reasonable chance of detecting a material fraud and other errors.

##  1.14 AUDIT EXPECTATION GAP

As per the definition of the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) in 1992, the expectation gap is "the difference between what the public and financial statement users believe auditors are responsible for and what auditors themselves believe their responsibilities are."
Expectation gap may arise on the performance level i.e. what users expect from auditor and how auditor actually performed.
Auditor is required to reduce audit risk to an acceptably low level to attain reasonable assurance. But the term "Reasonable Assurance" may itself be difficult to comprehend from the user's point of view and the auditor's point of view. This may also result in expectation gap.
Example: The users may not have the knowledge of objectives of audit. Therefore when the auditor is appointed, they may expect the auditor to identify all the misstatement (whether due to error or fraud). However, due to inherent limitations, it is not possible for the auditor to identify and report all the misstatements.
There are different other areas, that may lead to expectation gap. If an appropriate resolution can be identified for these areas, the gap may be decreased significantly. The following areas can be considered:



---

$\checkmark$ Users must understand about the inherent limitations of the audit 

$\checkmark$ Users must acknowledge their responsibility in absolute manner and not just as a formality 

$\checkmark$ Auditor's must communicate their responsibilities not just through Terms of Engagement and Audit Report but also should conduct seminars and workshops to make clear understanding. 

$\checkmark$ Before starting the audit, the auditor must have direct communication between the TCWG/ management etc. to understand whether they have specific expectations from the auditor and whether the auditor is in position to meet those expectations.

## 1.15 BASIC PRINCIPLES GOVERNING AN AUDIT/ASSURANCE

As per Sec. 100.5 of the Code of Ethics 2015, recommended by ICAN, A professional accountant shall comply with the following fundamental principles:

| Principles              | Duty                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Integrity               | $\checkmark$ To be straightforward and honest in all professional and business relationships.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| Objectivity             | $\checkmark$ To not allow bias, conflict of interest or undue influence of others to override professional or business judgments.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| Competence and Due Care | $\checkmark$ To maintain professional knowledge and skill at the level required to ensure that a client or employer receives competent professional service based on current developments in practice, legislation and techniques and act diligently and in accordance with applicable technical and professional standards.                                                                                     |
| Confidentiality         | $\checkmark$ To respect the confidentiality of information acquired as a result of professional and business relation- hips and, therefore, not disclose any such information to third parties without proper and specific authority, **unless there is a legal or professional right or duty to disclose**, nor use the information for the personal advantage of the professional accountant or third parties. |
| Professional Behavior   | $\checkmark$ To comply with relevant laws and regulations and avoid any action that discredits the profession.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

## 1.16 INHERENT LIMITATIONS OF AUDIT

$\Rightarrow$ "Inherent" means existing in something as a permanent, essential or characteristic attribute. $\Rightarrow$ Inherent Limitations of audit refer to those constraints that always exist and cannot be removed though can be reduced to certain level. $\Rightarrow$ Due to the presence of following inherent limitations of audit, auditor only expresses an opinion on the financial statements and cannot give the guarantee regarding the correctness of financial statements., time limitation, cost limitation

---

|                                             Limitations                                             |                                                                                                                                                                                                            Explanation                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------: | :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------: |
|                                      1. Test Checking sampling                                      |                                                                                       $\checkmark$ Auditor selects samples of transactions to check. <br> $\checkmark$ Due to the time constraints, auditor cannot check each and every transaction in detail thereby leaving a possibility that unchecked items may contain misstatements.                                                                                       |
|                                 2. Involvement of Judgment opinion                                  |                                                                                      $\checkmark$ The word "opinion" itself refers to the result of judgment of the auditor. <br> $\checkmark$ The Judgement of auditor depends upon his qualification and experience. <br> $\checkmark$ The judgement of auditor may not always be correct.                                                                                      |
| 3. Nature of Audit Evidence <br> Presuasive not conclusive \& Reasonable not atachile asurance only |                                  $\checkmark$ The audit evidences are persuasive rather than conclusive in nature. <br> $\checkmark$ They can only give a reasonable assurance about the validity of transaction but cannot give absolute assurance. <br> $\checkmark$ Sometimes the evidence may be (forged) by the management, which auditor may not detect. Ex: Fake Invoices and documents.                                   |
|                         4. Inherent Limitations of Internal Control System                          | $\checkmark$ The design and implementation of Internal Control System is ultimate responsibility of management. <br> $\checkmark$ Internal Control System itself suffers certain Limitations such as: <br> a . Cost Effectiveness, b. Unusual Transactions c. Change in conditions, d. Collusion among employees e. Potential of Human Error etc. <br> $\checkmark$ These Limitations affect the accounting system of the entity. |

## NSA 200 (Existing) 

Objective of an Audit (Para 5)
$\Rightarrow$ The objective of an audit of financial statements is to enable the auditor to express on opinion whether the financial statements are prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with an idenqified financial reporting framework.
$\Rightarrow$ The phrases used to express the auditor's opinion are "give a true and fair view" or "present fairly in all material respects" which are equivalent terms.
$\Rightarrow$ Although the auditor's opinion enhances the credibility of the financial statements, the user cannot assume that the opinion is an assurance as to the future viability of the entity nor the efficiency or effectiveness with which management has conducted the affairs of the entity.

---

Ethical principles governing the auditor's responsibilities/ Basic principles governing an audit (Para 6,7)
a. Integrity, Objectivity and Independence

- The auditor should be straight forward, honest and sincere in rendering professional services. The auditor must be fair and should not allow prejudice, bias or influence of others to override his/her objectivity.
- The auditor should be independent in fact and appearance
b. Professional Competence and Due Care
- The auditor should perform professional services with due care and competence and has a continuing duty to maintain professional knowledge and skill at a level required to ensure that the client receives the advantage of competent professional service.
a. Confidentiality
- The auditor should respect the confidentiality of information acquired during the course of performing professional services and should not use or disclose any such information without proper and specific authority or unless there is a legal or professional right or duty to disclose.
b. Professional Behavior
- The auditor should act in a manner consistent with the good reputation of the profession and refrain from any conduct that might bring discredit to the profession
c. Technical Standards
- The auditor should carry out professional services in accordance with the relevant technical and professional standards.
- Auditors have a duty to carry out with care and skill, instructions of clients insofar as they are compatible with the requirements of integrity, objectivity and independence.
- The auditor should conduct an audit in accordance with the Nepal Standards on Auditing (Para 8)
- The auditor should plan and perform the audit with an attitude of professional skepticism recognizing that circumstances may exist which cause the financial statements to be materially misstated (Para 9)

It may be conducted for other specific purposes such as admission of partner, valuation if business etc. |

---

| Continuous/ Concurrent Audit | $\Rightarrow$ In large organizations, it is not possible to conclude audit in short period of time after the books of accounts are closed (i.e end of FY), due to which the audit is conducted throughout the year till its completion. <br> $\Rightarrow$ This type of audit is known as continuous or concurrent audit. |
| Due Diligence Audit (DDA) | $\Rightarrow$ The audit which is conducted for viability of potential investment is known as Due Diligence Audit. <br> $\Rightarrow$ Generally DDA are conducted for mergers and acquisitions or similar potential investment plans. Different categories of Due Diligence are: <br> a. Financial Due Diligence <br> $\Rightarrow$ It is conducted to identify whether or not company accounts are consistent, evaluating the real situation of assets, liabilities and tax risks. <br> $\Rightarrow$ Financial due diligence ordinarily employs methods such as document review, conducting discussion and interviews with senior management and key employees, comparing historical financial data and trend analysis. <br> b. Legal Due Diligence <br> $\Rightarrow$ It is an analysis of contracts and other documents, evaluating whether or not any hidden legal hazards or lawsuits exist. <br> c. Human Resources due diligence <br> $\Rightarrow$ It is conducted for identification of the qualifications, technical ability and working initiative of the target firm's senior management personnel and key staff. <br> d. Operational Due Diligence <br> $\Rightarrow$ It is an evaluation of a target firm's business model and prospects, including identification of the existence of a market, whether or not the firm has an attractive force, and assessing their competitive situation. |

| A. Final Audit/ Periodical Audit/ Completed Audit                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | B. Continuous Audit                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Meaning:**<br>The audit which starts after the closure of books of accounts i.e. end of financial year and is continued till its completion is known as final audit.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | **Meaning:**<br>In large organizations, it is not possible to conclude audit in short period of time after the books of accounts are closed (i.e end of FY), due to which the audit is conducted throughout the year till its completion, this type of audit is known as continuous audit.<br>                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Advantages:**<br>1. It is less costly because the resources are used at once and for all.<br>2. The regular workflow of the client is not disturbed as the client is prepared for the audit at the end of the period.<br>3. There is less chance of manipulation in accounts because once the books of accounts are closed; it is not that easy to alter the financial figures.                                           | **Advantages:**<br>1. It is easier to detect the misstatements in timely manner.<br>2. There is regular update of the client's books of accounts.<br>3. It acts as a moral check on the clients staffs. Due to this, there is less chance that they commit the errors or frauds.<br>4. The suggestions can be provided and implemented in timely manner.<br>5. Preparation of financial statements is completed on timely basis.<br>6. The auditor has less pressure at the year end.<br> |
| **Disadvantages :**<br>1. Not suitable for large organizations due to volume of work.<br>2. Since there is less time to conclude the audit, it is difficult to detect the planned frauds.<br>3. There is possibility of ignoring errors as the auditor mainly depends upon the test checking (due to time constraints)<br>4. The auditor has excessive workload at the year end to conclude audit and issue the report.<br> | **Disadvantages :**<br>1. Chance of manipulation and alteration of accounts is higher.<br>2. The client's day to day work is disturbed because of the presence of the audit staff.<br>3. It is costlier as compared to the final audit.<br>4. Sometimes, the queries arisen during the audit may remain outstanding when the audit staff loses the sequence of the work conducted.                                                                                                        |
**Precautions to avoid the limitations (Disadvantages)**
$\checkmark$ There should be continuous monitoring of the work
$\checkmark$ The specific work should be completed before starting the other work.
$\checkmark$ The record must be kept for each stage of work completed, so that it can be reviewed and the remaining work can be conducted efficiently.
$\checkmark$ The management should be strictly enquired about the altered or manipulated figures.

## 1.19 STANDARDS ON AUDITING

$\Rightarrow$ Standards on Auditing (SA's) are sets of standards against which the quality of audits as performed and may be judged.
$\Rightarrow$ The SA's establish the overall objectives of the auditor, which are to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements as a whole are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, thus enabling the auditor to express an opinion on whether the financial statements are prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with an applicable financial reporting framework, or otherwise
$\Rightarrow$ They are a tool to manage the audit risk.

### INTERNATIONAL AUDITING AND ASSURANCE STANDARD BOARD (IAASB)

The International Federation of Accountants (IFAC) is the worldwide organization for the accountancy profession dedicated to serving the public interest by strengthening the profession and contributing to the development of strong international economies.
It was set up with the mission to bring harmony in the profession of accountancy across the world. The International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board (IAASB) is an independent standard body which issues standards, like the International Standards on Auditing, quality control guidelines and other services, to support the international auditing of financial statements. It is a body supported by IFAC.

The objectives of the IAASB include:
$\checkmark$ Supporting global financial stability
$\checkmark$ Enhancing the role, relevancy and quality of assurance in an evolving world
$\checkmark$ Facilitating adoption and implementation of the standards it sets.
The IAASB achieves these objectives by:
$\checkmark$ Establishing high quality auditing standards and guidance for financial statement audits.
$\checkmark$ Establishing high quality auditing standards and guidance for other types of assurance services and related services.
$\checkmark$ Publishing Guidelines and pronouncement to facilitate the assurance and related services in an efficient manner.

## 1.20 AUDITING STANDARDS BOARD (AuSB)

$\Rightarrow$ Auditing Standards Board (AuSB) has been constituted by the Government of Nepal on 26 Falgun 2059 corresponding to 10 March, 2003 under Nepal Chartered Accountants Act, 1997 (first amendment 2002).
$\Rightarrow$ The AuSB consists of 7 members comprising:
	$\checkmark$ A Chairman appointed by the Government of Nepal from Fellow Chartered Accountants
	$\checkmark$ Representative of Ministry of Finance(MoF),
	$\checkmark$ Representative of Office of the Auditor General(OAG),
	$\checkmark$ Three Chartered Accountants and
	$\checkmark$ One Registered Auditor nominated by the Government of Nepal on the recommendation of Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nepal (ICAN).
$\Rightarrow$ The board has full discretion in developing and pursuing the technical agenda for setting Auditing Standards.
$\Rightarrow$ While formulating NSA(s), the AuSB considers the applicable laws, customs, usages and business environments in Nepal. The NSAs are issued under the authority of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1997 (first amendment 2002).
$\Rightarrow$ The AuSB issues Guidance notes on the issues arising from the NSAs wherever necessary. AuSB reviews and revises the NSAs at periodical intervals or as per the need of the respective standards.
$\Rightarrow$ The AuSB determines the broad areas in which the NSAs need to be formulated and the priority in regard to the selection thereof.

### Functions of the Board
Pursuant to Section 3(kha) of Nepal Chartered Accountants Act, 1997, main functions of the Board are:
	$\checkmark$ Regulate and systematize auditing profession, formulation of auditing standards on the basis of International Standards on Auditing (ISA).
	$\checkmark$ Set procedures to develop auditing standards and publish materials related to auditing standards.
	$\checkmark$ Make improvement and revision of auditing standards in Ilne with International Standards on Auditing.
	$\checkmark$ Interpretation of auditing standards.
	$\checkmark$ Prepare guidance notes.
	$\checkmark$ Facilitate application and publicity of standards.


### Nepal Standards on Auditing Formulation Procedures

| Stages | Procedures |
| :--: | :--: |
| Stage I <br> Identification of Standards by the Board | $\checkmark$ The Board identifies relevant Standards and refers the secretariat to prepare the draft on those are Standards in line with International Standards on Auditing |
| Stage II <br> Preparation of Initial Draft and Submission in Board Meeting | $\checkmark$ The pre circulated draft is reviewed at the Board meeting for comments and suggestions. Several Board meetings may be required for preparation of an Exposure Draft |
| Stage III <br> Produce Exposure Draft and send to public, regulators and stakeholders for comments and opinion. | $\checkmark$ Collection and analysis of comments received on the Exposure Draft. |
| Stage IV <br> Board review the comments received for refinement and finalization of the Exposure Draft. | $\checkmark$ Final version of Standard forwarded to the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nepal for consideration by ICAN with recommended date for implementation. |

|      Annual financial statement       | (1) The following annual financial statements shall be prepared by the board of directors of a public company every year at least thirty days prior to the holding of its annual general meeting and in the case of a private company, within six months of the expiry of its financial year: <br> a. Balance sheet as at the last date of the financial year. <br> b. Profit and loss account of the financial year. <br> c. Description of cash flow of the financial year. <br> (2) This annual financial statement to be prepared pursuant to Sub-section(1) shall give true and fair view of the state of affairs of the company as at the last day of the financial year concerned and also state the account of profit and loss and description of cash flow made in that financial year. <br> Other Related Provisions <br> $\checkmark$ The annual financial statements and the report of board of directors prepared pursuant to this Section shall be approved by the board of directors and signed by the Chairperson of the board of directors and at least one director. <br> $\checkmark$ The accounts and annual financial statements prepared by a company pursuant to this Chapter shall be kept safely for at least five years after the date of expiry of the financial year concerned. <br> $\checkmark$ The officers who prepare any false annual financial statements, reports of board of directors and other returns and reports required to be prepared pursuant to this Act and the directors who approve the same shall be liable |

## 1.22 OTHER MATTERS 

### A. Relationship between Regulator and Auditor

- The external auditor has an important role to play in the regulatory framework, which requires confidence in audited financial information to ensure that supervisory efforts and policies are effective, appropriate and based on accurate data.
- This requires an open, co-operative and constructive relationship between the supervisor and the auditor so they can both provide effective input to the supervisory review.
- It is important, therefore, that the terms and scope of this relationship are clearly defined and understood by both parties and regulated firms.
- In context of Nepal, regulators like Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) and Insurance Boards have assumed the responsibility for supervision and regulation on financial sector.
- Management letters and long-form audit reports submitted by auditors can provide supervisors with valuable insight into various aspects of operations.
- As per the Supervisory Statement on The relationship between the external auditor and the supervisor: a code of practice (2013), issued by Bank of England, the following principles are laid establish the relationship between the Supervisors and the Auditors:

| Principle 1 | Supervisors and auditors shall seek an open and constructive relationship |
| :-- | :-- |
| Principle 2 | Supervisors and auditors should engage in regular dialogue. |
| Principle 3 | Supervisors and auditors shall share all information relevant to carrying out <br> their respective statutory duties in a timely fashion. |
| Principle 4 | Supervisors and auditors shall respect their duty to treat information shared <br> between the two parties or received from firms confidentially. |

The various circumstances where the proper communication between the regulator and the auditor is required may be:
$\checkmark$ Where the auditor becomes aware of facts which might endanger the existence of the entity (going concern)
$\checkmark$ Where either the auditor or the regulator detects an indication of fraud at a senior level
$\checkmark$ Where the auditor intends to resign in the course of an audit
$\checkmark$ Where the auditor has an irreconcilable difference of view with management over a material aspect of the financial statements, as a results of which he is intending to issue an audit opinion which is not unqualified
$\checkmark$ Where the regulator has information which can materially affect the financial statements or the auditor's report; and
$\checkmark$ Where the auditor believes a matter should be communicated to the regulator/supervisor and management has failed to make such communication when requested to do so. Licensing conditions have been complied with

Some example of relationship of regulator and ICAN
$\checkmark$ Joint meeting with ICAN/ASB regarding implementation of IFRS in banking sector
$\checkmark$ A committee is formed by the ICAN to make fully convergent to the directive no 4 where; NRB senior representative is also a member. This committee is formed on request of NRB.
$\checkmark$ An interaction program on branch audit concept was jointly organized with ICAN and NRB inviting Bankers at the premises of NRB.
$\checkmark$ Organizing informal meeting with the auditors regarding the accounting issues.

### B. Sarbanes- Oxley Act -2002 (SOX)

The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, also known as SOX, was passed due to the accounting scandals at Enron, WorldCom, Global Crossing, Tyco and Arthur Andersen, that resulted in billions of dollars in corporate and investor losses.
SOX lays strict regulations on corporate frauds. SOX created the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) to oversee the accounting industry, banned company loans to executives and gave job protection to whistleblowers.

#### Summary of certain scandals:

a. Enron Scandal
$\Rightarrow$ Enron Corporation was an American energy company based in Houston, Texas. CFO along with other executives was able to mislead BOD and audit committee by hiding billions of debt from failed deals.
$\Rightarrow$ The auditor's were pressurized to ignore the issues. The stock price was inflated and it hit $\$ 90$ per share in mid-2000. However, when the scandal was revealed, the value of the stock was less than $\$ 1$. Later on the company was declared bankrupt.
$\Rightarrow$ Their auditor's Arthur Anderson was also dissolved.
b. WorldCom Scandal
$\Rightarrow$ WorldCom was a U.S.-based telecommunications company was at one time the secondlargest long distance phone company in the U.S.
$\Rightarrow$ WorldCom made major accounting misstatements that hid the increasingly perilous financial condition of the company, inflating the company's assets by around $\$ 12$ billion dollars.
The auditors should therefore consider their responsibility of quality reporting and also consider their liability towards public, for the faith build upon the auditing profession.

## 1.23 NSA 200 <br> OVERALL OBJECTIVES OF THE INDEPENDENT AUDITOR AND THE CONDUCT OF AN AUDIT IN ACCORDANCE WITH NEPAL STANDARDS ON AUDITING

### Scope of this NSA

$\Rightarrow$ This Nepal Standard on Auditing (NSA) deals with the independent auditor's overall responsibilities when conducting an audit of financial statements in accordance with NSAs.
$\Rightarrow$ It also explains the scope, authority and structure of the NSAs, and includes requirements establishing the general responsibilities of the independent auditor.

### An Audit of Financial Statements

$\Rightarrow$ The purpose of an audit is to enhance the degree of confidence of intended users in the financial statements.
$\Rightarrow$ This is achieved by the expression of an opinion by the auditor on whether the financial statements are prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with an applicable financial reporting framework.
$\Rightarrow$ NSAs require the auditor to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements as a whole are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error.
$\Rightarrow$ The concept of materiality is applied by the auditor both in planning and performing the audit.
$\Rightarrow$ The NSAs require that the auditor exercise professional judgment and maintain professional skepticism throughout the planning and performance of the audit and, among other things:
	$\checkmark$ identify and assess risks of material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, based on an understanding of the entity and its environment, including the entity's internal control.
	$\checkmark$ Obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about whether material misstatements exist, through designing and implementing appropriate responses to the assessed risks.
	$\checkmark$ Form an opinion on the financial statements based on conclusions drawn from the audit evidence obtained.

### Overall Objectives of the Auditor 

The overall objectives of the auditor are:
a. To <u>obtain reasonable assurance</u> about whether the financial statements as a whole are free from material misstatement, and whether the financial statements are prepared in accordance with an applicable financial reporting framework; and
b. To <u>report</u> on the financial statements (i.e. express an opinion), and communicate as required by the NSAs, in accordance with the auditor's findings.
Note: In cases when reasonable assurance cannot be obtained and a qualified opinion is insufficient the auditor shall disclaim an opinion or withdraw (or resign) from the engagement.

### Definitions

a. Applicable financial reporting framework - The financial reporting framework adopted by management for the preparation of the financial statements that is consistent as per the nature of the business of the entity as required by law or regulation.
b. Audit evidence - Information used by the auditor in arriving at the conclusions on which the auditor's opinion is based. (i.e The basis of the auditors opinion)
	$\checkmark$ Sufficiency of audit evidence is the measure of the quantity of audit evidence.
	$\checkmark$ Appropriateness of audit evidence is the measure of the quality of audit evidence. (Such as Original PAN bills, VAT bills, expenses made with authority etc.)
c. Audit risk - The risk that the auditor expresses an inappropriate audit opinion when the financial statements are materially misstated.
Audit risk is a function of the risks of material misstatement and detection risk.
d. Auditor - The person qualified to act as an auditor.
e. Detection risk - The risk that the auditors procedures will not detect a misstatement that exists and that could be material, either individually or when aggregated with other misstatements.
 f. Historical financial information - information expressed in financial terms in relation to a particular entity, derived primarily from that entity's accounting system, about economic events occurring in past time
g. Management - The person(s) with executive responsibility for the conduct of the entity's
operations Eg: BOD, Managing Partners etc.
h. Misstatement - A difference between the amount, classification, presentation, or disclosure of a reported financial statement item and the amount, classification, presentation, or disclosure that is required for the item to be in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework.
Misstatements can arise from error or fraud.

## Responsibility of Management:

To provide the auditor with:
$\checkmark$ Access to all information of which management and, where appropriate, those charged with governance are aware that is relevant to the preparation of the financial statements such as records, documentation and other matters;
$\checkmark$ Additional information that the auditor may request from management and, where appropriate, those charged with governance for the purpose of the audit
$\checkmark$ Unrestricted access to persons within the entity from whom the auditor determines it necessary to obtain audit evidence.
i. Professional judgment - The application of relevant training, knowledge and experience, within the context provided by auditing, accounting and ethical standards, in making informed decisions about the courses of action that are appropriate in the circumstances of the audit engagement.
j. Professional skepticism - An attitude that includes a questioning mind, being alert to conditions which may indicate possible misstatement due to error or fraud, and a critical assessment of audit evidence.
k. Reasonable assurance - In the context of an audit of financial statements, a high, but not absolute, level of assurance.
I. Risk of material misstatement - The risk that the financial statements are materially misstated prior to audit. This consists of two components, described as follows at the assertion level;
	(i) Inherent risk - The susceptibility of an assertion about a class of transaction, account balance or disclosure to a misstatement that could be material, either individually or when aggregated with other misstatements, before consideration of any related controls.
	(ii) Control risk - The risk that a misstatement that could occur in an assertion about a class of transaction, account balance or disclosure and that could be material, either individually or when aggregated with other misstatements, will not be prevented, or detected and corrected, on a timely basis by the entity's internal control.
m. Those charged with governance - The person(s) or organization(s) with responsibility for overseeing the strategic direction of the entity and obligations related to the accountability of the entity.

---

Requirements /objectives of auditor
A. Ethical Requirements Relating to an Audit of Financial Statements
	$\checkmark$ The auditor shall comply with relevant ethical requirements, including those relating to independence, relating to financial statement audit engagements.
B. Professional Skepticism
	$\checkmark$ The auditor shall plan and perform an audit with professional skepticism recognizing that circumstances may exist that cause the financial statements to be materially misstated.
C. Professional Judgment
	$\checkmark$ The auditor shall exercise professional judgment in planning and performing an audit of financial statements.
D. Sufficient Appropriate Audit Evidence and Audit Risk
	$\checkmark$ To obtain reasonable assurance, the auditor shall obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to reduce audit risk to an acceptably low level and thereby enable the auditor to draw reasonable conclusions on which to base the auditor's opinion.
E. Conduct of an Audit in Accordance with NSAs
	$\checkmark$ The auditor shall comply with all NSAs relevant to the audit.

Failure to Achieve an Objective
If an objective in a relevant NSA cannot be achieved, the auditor shall evaluate whether this prevents the auditor from achieving the overall objectives of the auditor
If YES $\rightarrow$ Modify the Opinion
OR
Withdraw From the engagement.

Answer:
Factors which may cause risk in conducting an audit are discussed below
i. Exercising judgement on the part of the auditor: The auditor's work irtif
exercise of judgement, for example, in deciding the extent of audit procedi. and in assessing the reasonableness of the judgements and estimates made
management in preparing the financial statements.
ii. Nature of audit evidence: Much of the evidence available to the auditor carl erith him to draw only conclusion there from. The auditor normally relies upon persua. evidence rather than conclusive evidence. Even in circumstances where conil. evidence is available, the cost of obtaining such evidence may far exceed the benefits.
iii. Inherent limitations of internal control: Internal controls can provide only reasonable but not absolute, assurance on account of several inherent limitations such as potential for human error, possibility of circumstances of control through collusion, etc.
On accounts of above, it is quite clear that an audit suffers from control risk on account of inherent limitation of internal control and detection risk on account of test rature of audit and judgement and estimates involve in formulating accounting policies.


2. Mention briefly the condition or event, which increase the risk of fraud or error leading to material misstatement in Financial Statements.

Answer:
Conditions or event which increase the risk of fraud or error are:
i. Weaknesses in the design of internal control system and non-compliance with the laid down control procedures, e.g., a single person is responsible for multiple functions.
ii. Doubts about the integrity or competence of the management, e.g., domination by one person, high turnover rate of employees, frequent change of legal counsels or auditors, significant and prolonged understaffing of the accounts department, etc.
iii. Unusual pressure within the entity, for example, industry s doing well but the company is not performing accordingly, heavy dependence on a single line of product, inadequate working capital, entity needs raising share prices to support the market price in the wake of public offer, etc.
iv. Unusual transaction such as transactions with related parties, excessive payment for certain services to lawyers, etc.
v. Problems in obtaining sufficient and appropriate audit evidence, e.g., inadequate documentation, significant differences between the figures as per the accounting records and confirmation received from third parties, etc.


3. Write short notes of "Process of Judgment formation by the auditor."

Answer:
After the audit, the opinion that the auditor expresses is the result of exercise of judgment on facts, evidence and circumstances which he comes across in the course of audit. The judgment is formed on the following basis:
$\checkmark$ Identification of the assertions to be examined.
$\checkmark$ Evaluation of the assertions as to felatly importance.
$\checkmark$ Collection of the information or evidence about the assertions to enable him to give an informed opinion.
$\checkmark$ Evaluation of evidence as valid or invalid/pertinent/ sufficient, or insufficient.

# Chapter 2: ASSURANCE

## 2.1 MEANING OF ASSURANCE

The term assurance refers to the expression of a conclusion that is intended to increase the confidence that users can place in a given subject matter or information. For example, an auditor's report is a conclusion that increases the confidence that users can place in a company's financial statements. Without assurance from the auditors, the shareholders may not accept that the information provided by the financial statements is sufficiently accurate and reliable.

✓ Assurance is a broader term than audit. An audit engagement is an assurance engagement but not all the assurance engagements are audit engagements.

'Assurance' means confidence. In an assurance engagement, an 'assurance firm' is engaged by one party to give an opinion on a piece of information that has been prepared by another party.

Assurance can be provided by:
a. Audit : It may be external audit, internal audit or a combination of the two.
b. Review : It may be review of financial information or specific element of financial statement

Examples of Assurance Services are:
- An audit of Financial Statements
- A review of Financial Statements
- Risk Assessment Reports
- System Reliability Reports
- Reports on Social and Environmental issues

## 2.2 TYPES OF ASSURANCE

1. Reasonable Assurance
	→ A <u>high (but not absolute) level of assurance</u> provided by the practitioner's conclusion expressed in a positive form.
	→ In a reasonable assurance engagement, the practitioner:
	- Gathers sufficient appropriate evidence to be able to draw reasonable conclusions;
	- Concludes that the subject matter conforms in all material respects with identified suitable criteria; and
	- Gives a positively worded assurance opinion.


2. Limited Assurance
	→ A moderate level of assurance provided by the practitioner's conclusion expressed in a negative form.
	→ In a limited assurance assignment the practitioner:
	- Gathers sufficient appropriate evidence to be able to draw limited conclusions;
	- Concludes that the subject matter, with respect to identified suitable criteria, is plausible in the circumstances; and
	- Gives a negatively worded assurance opinion.


## 2.3 COMPARISON CHART

|  Type of Assurance | Example | Nature of key work | Wordings of Opinion  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  Reasonable assurance (POSITIVE LEVEL) | An audit of financial statement | Detailed testing, evidence gathering and substantiation to support the conclusion. | "In our opinion, The Financial Statements give a True & Fair View"  |
|  Limited assurance (NEGATIVE LEVEL) | A review of financial statements | Primarily enquiries and analysis, less detailed procedure | "Nothing has come to our attention that causes us to believe that Financial Statements are materially mis-stated"  |

![img-0.jpeg](assets/audit%20book%20ch2,3_img-0.jpeg)

## 2.4 ELEMENTS OF ASSURANCE


1. A Three Party Relationship
	**i. Practitioner :**
	✓ The term "practitioner" as used in this Framework is broader than the term "auditor" as used in NSAs and NSREs, which relates only to practitioners performing audit or review engagements with respect to historical financial information.
	✓ A practitioner may be requested to perform assurance engagements on a wide range of subject matters. Some subject matters may require specialized skills and knowledge beyond those ordinarily possessed by an individual practitioner.
	✓ Example: the audit firm in a statutory audit (auditor)  
	-
	**ii. A Responsible Party :**
	The Person(s) who:
	e. In directing a reporting engagement, is responsible for the subject matter:
	OR
	f. In the assertion based engagement, is responsible for the subject matter information and may be responsible for subject matter.
	✓ Example: the Directors are responsible for preparing the financial statements to be audited
	✓ The responsible party may or may not be the party who engages the practitioner.  
	-
	**iii. Users** 
	✓ The person(s) or class of persons for whom the practitioner prepares the assurance report.
	✓ Example: The shareholders in a statutory audit  



2. An Appropriate Subject Matter 
	✓ It is the data that have been prepared by the responsible party for the practitioner to evaluate. It may constitute various forms such as:
	a. Financial Performance or conditions such as Financial Statements, Cash Flow Statements etc.
	b. Non Financial Performance or conditions such as Operational Review etc.
	c. Systems and Processes such as Internal Control System, IT related system etc.
	✓ An appropriate subject matter is:
	a. Identifiable, and capable of consistent evaluation or measurement against the identified criteria; and
	b. Such that the information about it can be subjected to procedures for gathering sufficient appropriate evidence.  

3. Suitable criteria 
	✓ It is the benchmark against which the subject matter is evaluated.
	✓ For example: Accounting Standards, Financial Reporting Framework, Company Laws etc.
	• When reporting on financial statements, the Financial Reporting Standards.
	• When reporting on internal control, the criteria may be an established internal control framework.
	• When reporting on compliance, the criteria may be the applicable law, regulation or contract.
	Suitable criteria exhibit the following characteristics:
	**Relevance:**
	✓ Relevant criteria contribute to conclusions that assist decision-making by the intended users.
	**Completeness:**
	✓ Criteria are sufficiently complete when they include all relevant factors that could affect the conclusions.
	**Reliability**
	✓ Reliable criteria allow reasonably consistent evaluation of the subject matter.
	**Neutrality**
	✓ Neutral criteria so that conclusions that are free from bias.
	**Understandability**
	✓ Conclusions that are clear, comprehensive, and not subject to significantly different interpretations  



4. Sufficient Appropriate Evidence 
	✓ It is the information used by the practitioner in arriving at the conclusion on which their opinion is based. This must be sufficient (quantity) and appropriate (quality).
	✓ The practitioner considers materiality, engagement risk and appropriateness of evidence in determining NTE of evidence gathering procedures.  

5. Assurance Report 
	✓ The report (normally written) containing the practitioner’s opinion.
	✓ This is issued to the intended user following the collection of evidence.
	✓ For Example: Audit Report in Statutory Audit
