# Chapter 8: AUDIT DOCUMENTATION

In it should be kept safe for 5 years.
In regard to prepared up to 60 days after completion of audit

## 8.1 INTRODUCTION

- Audit working papers are the documents which record all audit evidence obtained during the course of the audit.

- The working papers provide documented evidence of an examination and evaluation and provide a connecting link between the work which is performed and the final audit report.

- The working papers generally give knowledge about the planning, procedures performed, evidence obtained and conclusions drawn in the course of the audit. The working papers are standardized, dated and signed.

- The use of standardized working papers (for example, checklists, specimen letters, organization of working papers) may improve the efficiency with which such working papers are prepared and reviewed.

- Auditor should document the working papers in proper manner and if the working papers are in electronic media, he should take proper care for backup and safety.

- They show that:
	- ☑ The audit was properly planned and carried out
	- ☑ There was adequate supervision and
	- ☑ The evidence is sufficient and appropriate to support the audit opinion


### Advantages of Working Papers 

☑ It is necessary for reviewing quality controls
☑ It acts as basis for study of patterns and trends.
☑ It helps to guide the internal audit staff’s professional development.
☑ It provides supporting material for use in discussion with operating personnel.
☑ It acts as a source of evidence in litigations and lawsuit.
☑ It provides a basis for supervisory review and evaluation of audit performance.
☑ It is a permanent record for use in planning and carrying out future audits.
☑ It shows that the auditors have conducted the audit as per governing principles.  


### Confidentiality 

As a rule of confidentiality, the auditor must retain the working papers in an appropriate manner.

He should not show his working papers to anyone or disclose the confidential information obtained during the course of the audit.

However, he may disclose the information :
a. If permitted by the client
OR.
b. If required by the laws and regulations.  


### Custody of working papers 

Working Papers are the property of the auditor.
The auditor should retain working papers for the specified period.
The client does not have right to access the working paper of the auditor.
However the auditor may, at his discretion, provide copies or extracts of his working papers, if the request of the client is reasonable.
no one (except court)  

### Stack of Unnecessary Information 

The auditor should not prepare working papers in such a manner that he ends up having a pile of unnecessary information.
He should keep only those working papers that will serve an essential or useful purpose.
Useful purpose may be for future reference or for the purpose of statutory obligations.  


### Inclusion in working papers 

**Working papers normally include:**
1. Information concerning the legal and organizational structure of the client, MDA, ADA, SH register
2. Extracts or copies of important legal documents, agreements and minutes meeting report acts
3. Information concerning the industry economic environment and legislative environment within which the client operates,
4. Evidence of the planning process including audit programs and any changes thereto,
5. Evidence of the auditor’s understanding of the accounting and internal control systems,
6. Evidence of inherent and control risk assessments and any revisions thereof,
7. Evidence of the auditor’s consideration of the work of internal auditing and conclusions reached,
8. Analysis of transactions and balances,
9. Analysis of significant ratios and trends,
10. A record of the nature, timing and extent of audit procedures performed and the results of such procedures.  


### Retention of Working Papers 
The working papers should be retained for the period of 5 years from the date of auditor’s report.  


## 8.2 TYPES OF AUDIT FILES

![[2fcdcd0e-14.png]]

![[2fcdcd0e-15.png]]

https://youtu.be/Mt6vYltUDvY?t=323&si=JLi0cPadD-fmiiBv

Generally two types of Audit Files are maintained

a. Permanent File &
b. Current Audit File

### Permanent Audit File 

It includes the following:
1. Information concerning the legal and organizational structure of the client. In the case of a company, this includes the Memorandum and Articles of Association. In the case of a statutory corporation, this includes the Act and Regulations under which the corporation functions,
2. Extracts or copies of important legal documents, agreements and minutes relevant to the audit,
3. A record of the study and evaluation of the internal controls related to the accounting system. This might be in the form of narrative descriptions, questionnaires or flow charts, or some combination thereof,
4. Copies of audited financial statements of previous years, audited FS 49 PY
5. Analysis of significant ratios and trends,
6. Copies of management letters issued by the auditor, if any.
7. Record of communication with the retiring auditor, if any before acceptance of the appointment as auditor,
8. Notes regarding significant accounting policies and
9. Significant audit observations of earlier years.  


### Current Audit File 

It Include the following:
1. Correspondence relating to acceptance of annual reappointment,
2. Extracts of important matters in the minutes of Board Meetings and General Meetings, as are relevant to audit,
3. Evidence of the planning process of the audit and audit program,
4. Analysis of transactions and balances,
5. A record of the nature, timing and extent of auditing procedures performed, and the results of such procedures,
6. Evidence that the work performed by assistants was supervised and reviewed,
7. Copies of communications with other auditors, experts and other third parties,
8. Copies of letters or notes concerning audit matters communicated to or discussed with the client, including the terms of the engagement and material weaknesses in relevant internal controls,
9. Letters of representation or confirmation received from the client,
10. Conclusions reached by the auditor concerning significant aspects of the audit, including the manner in which exceptions and unusual matters, if any, disclosed by the auditor’s procedures were resolved or treated and
11. Copies of the financial information being reported on and the related audit reports.  |




### Audit Note Book

During the course of the audit, the audit staff may identify significant matters, errors, difficulties, etc. which need to be discussed and sorted out with the management etc. The Notebook that records all those matters which are not solved immediately and requires further explanations is known as audit notebook.

**Contents of Audit Note Book**
- ☑ The detail of the auditee and period of audit
- ☑ Names of officers and their responsibilities
- ☑ Routine queries such as missing invoices, clerical errors, wrong accounting etc.
- ☑ The effect of errors
- ☑ Irregularities in Financial Statements
- ☑ Deficiencies in internal control system
- ☑ Important matters for future reference


**Advantages/Usefulness of Audit Note Book**
- ☑ Helpful to prepare audit report
- ☑ The evaluation of audit staff can be done
- ☑ Matters to be discussed are not overlooked or ignored
- ☑ Helps to plan recurring audits
- ☑ Useful for the auditor to act as a defense if the charges of negligence are brought against him.

## 8.3 NSA 230 AUDIT DOCUMENTATION

### Introduction

#### Scope of this NSA (Para 1)

This NSA deals with the auditor's responsibility to prepare audit documentation for an audit of financial statements.

#### Nature and Purposes of Audit Documentation 
https://youtu.be/Mt6vYltUDvY?t=174&si=18ZqIVQ4c0dt8ElO

Audit documentation that meets the requirements of this NSA and the specific documentation requirements of other relevant NSAs provides:

a. Evidence of the auditor's basis for a conclusion about the achievement of the overall objective of the auditor; and
b. Evidence that the audit was planned and performed in accordance with NSAs and applicable legal and regulatory requirements.

#### Advantages of Audit Documentation 70
https://youtu.be/Mt6vYltUDvY?t=219&si=mZ2ha8TvH3zfH_Js

Audit documentation serves a number of additional purposes, including the following:

- ☑ Assisting the engagement team to plan and perform the audit.
- ☑ Assisting members of the engagement team responsible for supervision to direct and supervise the audit work, and to discharge their review responsibilities in accordance with NSA 220.
- ☑ Enabling the engagement team to be accountable for its work.
- ☑ Retaining a record of matters of continuing significance to future audits.
- Enabling the conduct of quality control reviews and inspections in accordance with NSQC 1 or national requirements that are at least as demanding.
- Enabling the conduct of external inspections in accordance with applicable legal, regulatory or other requirements.

### Objective (Para 8) 
https://youtu.be/Mt6vYltUDvY?t=174&si=18ZqIVQ4c0dt8ElO

The objective of the auditor is to prepare documentation that provides:

a. A sufficient and appropriate record of the basis for the auditor’s report; and
b. Evidence that the audit was planned and performed in accordance with NSAs and applicable legal and regulatory requirements.

### Definitions (Para 9)

a. Audit documentation – The record of audit procedures performed, relevant audit evidence obtained, and conclusions the auditor reached (terms such as “working papers” or “work papers” are also sometimes used).

b. Audit file – One or more folders or other storage media, *in physical or electronic form*, containing the records that comprise the audit documentation for a specific engagement.

c. Experienced auditor – An individual (whether internal or external to the firm) who has practical audit experience, and a reasonable understanding of:
	i. Audit processes;
	ii. NSAs and applicable legal and regulatory requirements;
	iii. The business environment in which the entity operates; and
	iv. Auditing and financial reporting issues relevant to the entity’s industry.

### Requirements

**a. Timely Preparation of Audit Documentation**
	☑ The auditor shall prepare audit documentation on a timely basis.
	☑ Documentation prepared after the audit work has been performed is likely to be less accurate than documentation prepared at the time such work is performed

#### Documentation of the Audit Procedures Performed and Audit Evidence Obtained

##### Form, Content and Extent of Audit Documentation
https://youtu.be/Mt6vYltUDvY?t=405&si=FsYbBzexbNW8UGSf

The auditor shall prepare audit documentation that is sufficient to enable an experienced auditor, having no previous connection with the audit, to understand:

a. The NTE of the audit procedures performed to comply with the NSAs and applicable legal and regulatory requirements;
b. The results of the audit procedures performed, and the audit evidence obtained; and
c. Significant matters arising during the audit, the conclusions reached thereon, and significant professional judgments made in reaching those conclusions.


##### Completion Memorandum / Audit Documentation Summary
https://youtu.be/Mt6vYltUDvY?t=908&si=0Eb_DzMqygYn-smx

The auditor may consider it helpful to prepare and retain as part of the audit documentation a summary (sometimes known as a completion memorandum) that describes the significant matters identified during the audit and how they were addressed, or that includes cross-references to other relevant supporting audit documentation that provides such information.

Such a summary may facilitate effective and efficient reviews and inspections of the audit documentation, particularly for large and complex audits.

Further, the preparation of such a summary may assist the auditor’s consideration of the significant matters. It may also help the auditor to consider whether, in light of the audit procedures performed and conclusions reached, there is any individual relevant NSA objective that the auditor cannot achieve that would prevent the auditor from achieving the overall objectives of the auditor.

##### The form, content and extent of audit documentation depend on factors such as:
https://youtu.be/Mt6vYltUDvY?t=630&si=T4iKRO8fiKKgjCRu

- ☑ The size and complexity of the entity.
- ☑ The nature of the audit procedures to be performed.
- ☑ The identified risks of material misstatement.
- ☑ The significance of the audit evidence obtained.
- ☑ The nature and extent of exceptions identified.

In documenting the NTE of audit procedures performed, the auditor shall record:
	a. The identifying characteristics of the specific items or matters tested;
	b. Who performed the audit work and the date such work was completed; and
	c. Who reviewed the audit work performed and the date and extent of such review.

The auditor shall document discussions of significant matters with management, TCWG, and others, including the nature of the significant matters discussed and when and with whom the discussions took place.

If the auditor identified information that is inconsistent with the auditor’s final conclusion regarding a significant matter, the auditor shall document how the auditor addressed the inconsistency.

Departure from a Relevant Requirement

If, in exceptional circumstances, the auditor judges it necessary to depart from a relevant requirement in an NSA, the auditor shall document how the alternative audit procedures performed achieve the aim of that requirement, and the reasons for the departure.

##### Matters Arising after the Date of the Auditor’s Report

If, in exceptional circumstances, the auditor performs new or additional audit procedures or draws new conclusions after the date of the auditor’s report, the auditor shall document:

a. The circumstances encountered;
b. The new or additional audit procedures performed, audit evidence obtained, and conclusions reached, and their effect on the auditor’s report; and
c. When and by whom the resulting changes to audit documentation were made and reviewed.


##### Assembly of the Final Audit File
https://youtu.be/Mt6vYltUDvY?t=760&si=wg4jb33oHzVHzbMZ

The auditor shall assemble the audit documentation in an audit file and complete the administrative process of assembling the final audit file on a timely basis after the date of the auditor's report.

- ☑ An appropriate time limit within which to complete the assembly of the final audit file is ordinarily not more than 60 days after the date of the auditor's report.
- ☑ Minimum retention period of audit file is 5 years from the date of auditor's report.

<u>Points to Remember</u>
- ☑ Working Papers means documents relating to audit, which is base for the auditors opinion and helpful for future reference.
- ☑ Working Papers are the property of the auditor, hence he is not bound to give them to anyone including client unless the justifiable request is made by the client. However, he must provide extracts (copies) of working papers and retain the original ones.
- ☑ Two types of Audit files are Permanent Audit File and Current Audit File.
- ☑ Final Audit File to be maintained within 60 days after date of audit report.
- ☑ Documentation to be retained upto 5 yrs from the date of audit report.

The form and content of working papers are affected by matters such as the:
- ☑ nature of the engagement,
- ☑ form of the auditor's report,
- ☑ nature and complexity of the client's business,
- ☑ nature and condition of the client's records and degree of reliance on internal control,
- ☑ needs in the particular circumstances for direction, supervision and review of work performed by assistants and
- ☑ specific audit methodology and technology used in the course of the audit

The form, content and extent of audit documentation depend on factors such as:
- ☑ The size and complexity of the entity.
- ☑ The nature of the audit procedures to be performed.
- ☑ The identified risks of material misstatement.
- ☑ The significance of the audit evidence obtained.
- ☑ The nature and extent of exceptions identified.

# Chapter 9 : INTERNAL CONTROL SYSTEM

## 9.1 MEANING

→ An organization has to design *strong and effective plans, policies, rules and regulations in order to conduct its business transactions in an effective manner*. Without proper rules and regulations, it becomes difficult to organize the transactions and conduct the operations of the business.

→ These rules and regulations are primarily known as Internal Control System.

→ Internal control can help an entity achieve its performance and profitability targets, and prevent loss of resources. It can help ensure reliable financial reporting. It can help ensure that the enterprise complies with laws and regulations, avoiding damage to its reputation and other consequences.

→ Those rules and regulations may be operational or financial.

**Operational control systems** are designed to ensure that day-to-day actions are consistent with established plans and objectives.

Corrective action is taken where performance does not meet standards. This action may involve training, motivation, leadership, discipline, or termination.

**Financial control systems** are designed to ensure that the financial transactions are conducted and recorded appropriately so that any misstatement, manipulation or misappropriation is identified, prevented or corrected in timely basis.

### Meaning of Internal Control System (NSA 315) 

![[2fcdcd0e-31.png]]

https://youtu.be/bea_M4AW6Xs?t=3162&si=zGFktP_zOav3samI

→ The process designed, implemented and maintained by those charged with governance, management and other personnel to provide reasonable assurance about the achievement of an entity’s objectives with regard to reliability of financial reporting, effectiveness and efficiency of operations, and compliance with applicable laws and regulations.

→ The term “controls” refers to any aspects of one or more of the components of internal control.  


### Definition of Internal Control System as per COSO framework 
→ A process, effected by the entity's board of directors, management and other personnel, designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the achievement of objectives', in three particular areas:
a. Effectiveness and efficiency of operations.
b. Reliability of financial reporting.
c. Compliance with applicable laws and regulations.

This definition emphasizes that internal control is:
☑ Geared to the achievement of objectives in one or more separate but overlapping categories
☑ A process consisting of ongoing tasks and activities—it is a means to an end, not an end in itself
☑ Affected by people—it is not merely about policy and procedure manuals, systems, and forms, but about people and the actions they take at every level of an organization to effect internal control
☑ Able to provide reasonable assurance, not absolute assurance, to an entity's senior management and board of directors
☑ Adaptable to the entity structure—flexible in application for the entire entity or for a particular subsidiary, division, operating unit, or business process.  



### Dimensions of Internal Control System 
The two dimensions of internal controls are
a. Administrative controls (operational controls):
These are related to:
☑ operations of the entity,
☑ administrative functions, and
☑ management decision making process

b. Accounting controls (financial controls)
These are related to:
☑ Safeguarding of assets and physical verification
☑ Reliability of financial records,
☑ Recording of transactions,
☑ Compliance with applicable financial reporting framework,
☑ Selection of appropriate accounting policies,
☑ Prevention, detection and correction of misstatements in timely manner  



### Objective of Internal Control System 
a. To ensure the orderly and efficient conduct of business in respect of systems being in place and fully implemented.
b. Prompt recording of transactions in appropriate account, in proper period, at correct amount.
c. To safeguard the assets of the business from misappropriation or manipulation.
d. To prevent and detect fraud in timely manner.
e. To ensure the completeness and accuracy of accounting records.
f. To ensure the timely preparation of financial information so that the results of the business are assessed in timely manner for decision making.  


### Scope of Internal Control System 
Scope of Internal control system extends beyond accounting controls.
It includes administrative controls and decision making process such as pricing policies, quality control, budgetary control etc.
The other functions included are:

a. Control Environment
It includes:
☑ The functions of the board of directors and committees.
☑ Management’s philosophy and operating cycle.
☑ The entity’s organizational structure and methods of assigning authority.
☑ Management’s control system such as segregation of duties.

b. Control Procedures
Control Procedures are those policies and procedures in addition to the control environment which are established to achieve the entity’s specific objectives.
It includes:
☑ Reporting, reviewing and approving reconciliations.
☑ Checking the arithmetical accuracy of the records.
☑ Access to data files.
☑ Maintaining and reviewing control accounts and trial balance.
☑ Limiting the direct access to assets and records.
☑ Comparing the results of cash, security and stock counts with accounting records.
However auditor is mainly concerned with financial controls.  


### Responsibility for Internal Control System 
→ The Management or those charged with governance are ultimately responsible for the system of internal control.
→ Those charged with governance will normally delegate to management the task of establishing, operating and monitoring the system. However the delegation of responsibility doesn't relieve the delegating authority from their liability.
→ The management should set appropriate policies on internal control and regularly assure itself that appropriate processes are functioning effectively to monitor the risks to which the company is exposed and that the system of internal control is effective in reducing those risks to an acceptable level.
→ The management or those charged with governance should send out a clear message that control responsibilities must be taken seriously.  


## 9.2 COMPONENT OF INTERNAL CONTROL SYSTEM

![img-0.jpeg](assets/audit%20book%20ch8,9_img-0.jpeg)

![[2fcdcd0e-31.png]]

![[2fcdcd0e-32.png]]


https://youtu.be/bea_M4AW6Xs?t=3771&si=G5uQ2VzhNjUCJqSS


## 1. Control Environment

- It is an overall attitude of people in the entity towards the internal control system.
- It is the foundation for all other components of internal control, providing discipline and structure.

![img-1.jpeg](assets/audit%20book%20ch8,9_img-1.jpeg)



- Control environment factors include the integrity, ethical values and competence of the entity's people; management's philosophy and operating style; the way management assigns authority and responsibility, and organizes and develops its people; and the attention and direction provided by the board of directors.
- It is this control environment that keeps anyone in the entity from committing any wrong doing.
- An auditor is required to obtain understanding whether such environment has been developed by management through its management philosophy and behavior in the entity.
- Control environment constitutes following elements:
- Communication and enforcement of integrity and ethical values
- Commitment to competence.
- Participation by TCWG
- Management's philosophy and operating style
- Organizational structure
- Assignment of authority and responsibility.


### 2. Control Activities 
Control activities are the policies and procedures that help ensure management directives are carried out.
They help ensure that necessary actions are taken to address risks to achievement of the entity's objectives.
Control activities that may be relevant to an audit may be categorized as policies and procedures that pertain to the following:
☑ Performance reviews such as budget analysis, internal and external data comparison etc.
☑ Information processing including IT controls.
☑ Physical controls that include access to assets, computer programs, periodic comparison of assets etc.
☑ Segregation of duties such as assigning responsibilities and specific functions to individuals.  



### 3. Entity's Risk Assessment Procedure 

Risk assessment is the identification and analysis of relevant risks to achievement of the objectives, forming a basis for determining how the risks should be managed.
Because economic, industry, regulatory and operating conditions will continue to change, mechanisms are needed to identify and deal with the special risks associated with change.
For example, the entity's risk assessment process may address how the entity considers the possibility of unrecorded transactions or identifies and analyzes significant estimates recorded in the financial statements.
Risks can arise due to following factors:
☑ Changes in operating environment.
☑ New personnel.
☑ New or revamped information systems
☑ Significant and rapid expansion of operations
☑ New technology.
☑ New business models, products, or activities.
☑ Corporate restructurings..
☑ Expanded foreign operations.
☑ New accounting pronouncements  

### 4. Monitoring of Controls 
Internal control systems need to be monitored. Monitoring is a process that assesses the quality of the system's performance over time.
This is accomplished through ongoing monitoring activities, separate evaluations or a combination of the two.
Ongoing monitoring occurs in the course of operations. It includes regular management and supervisory activities, and other actions personnel take in performing their duties.  


### 5. Information System, Including the Related Business Processes, Relevant to Financial Reporting, and Communication 

→ All personnel must receive a clear message from top management that control responsibilities must be taken seriously.
→ They must understand their own role in the internal control system, as well as how individual activities relate to the work of others.
→ They must have a means of communicating significant information upstream.
→ There also needs to be effective communication with external parties, such as customers, suppliers, regulators and shareholders.
→ The information system relevant to financial reporting objectives, which includes the financial reporting system, encompasses methods and records that:
✓ Identify and record all valid transactions.
✓ Permit proper classification of transactions for financial reporting.
✓ Measure the value of transactions in a manner that permits recording their proper monetary value in the financial statements.
✓ Determine the time period in which transactions occurred to permit recording of transactions in the proper accounting period.
✓ Present properly the transactions and related disclosures in the financial statements.
→ Communication also can be made electronically, orally, and through the actions of management.  


## 9.3 INHERENT LIMITATIONS OF INTERNAL CONTROL SYSTEM

The existence of internal control system in the entity doesn't guarantee regarding good governance of error free financial statements.

An internal control system, no matter how well conceived and operated, can provide only reasonable not absolute assurance to management and the board regarding achievement of an entity's objectives due to the inherent limitations that it possesses.


|                                             |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1. Cost Effectiveness                       | → The best control systems may not be available at the low costs.→ Internal controls must be cost effective, the result of a cost-benefit analysis. This leads to the implementation of the best system that can be afforded, which is not necessarily the best available internal control system for a specific situation. |
| 2. Unresponsive to changing circumstances.  | → In a diversified business environment, the existing internal control systems may remain unresponsive. <br>→ Due to this the changed business environment may not allow the control mechanism to detect the complex or new loopholes.                                                                                      |
| 3. Collusion among employees                | → Lack of integrity and dishonesty of employees and officials can lead to collusion amongst two or more people to circumvent the internal control system.                                                                                                                                                                   |
| 4. Complexity.                              | → An increasingly complex internal control system can lead to operational inefficiencies, because employees are unable to cope with the system.                                                                                                                                                                             |
| 5. Lack of communication.                   | → A lack of proper communication regarding internal control procedures, benefits, needs and responsibilities from the “top”, as well as the reporting of weaknesses and problems from the “bottom” have an adverse effect on the success of the internal control system.                                                    |
| 6. Human Error                              | → The effectiveness of the internal control system depends on the competence, reliability and due care of the people responsible for its operation.<br>→ Mistakes/errors threaten the effectiveness of any internal control system                                                                                          |
| 7. Override by management and/or executives | → Because of the authority and responsibility of officials high up in the organizational structure, the risk pervades that they can easily override the internal control system.                                                                                                                                            |
| 8. Illusion of control                      | → Managers create an illusion of control, while control procedures are circumvented and misinterpreted.<br>→ Management may not follow rules and regulations effectively but creates the illusion that everything is functioning as it should be.                                                                           |


## 9.4 EVALUATION OF INTERNAL CONTROL SYSTEM

### Meaning of Evaluation 
→ Evaluation means review of process and policies designed by the entity for achieving its objectives.
→ Evaluation is mainly concerned with understanding the suitability of internal control system as adopted by the entity and its operating effectiveness.
→ Operating effectiveness means the ability of the internal control system to prevent, correct and detect the misstatements on timely basis.  


### Objective of evaluation of internal control system 
→ The main objective behind evaluation of internal control system is to identify and establish the reliance that he can place thereon in determining the nature timing and extent of the substantive procedures.
→ Based upon compliance procedures if the auditor determines that internal control system is effective, and then the auditor may reduce his time for substantive procedures.  

### Benefits/ Advantages of review 
It helps the auditor to:
✓ Determine operating effectiveness of internal control system,
✓ Determine the areas which require detailed examination,
✓ Identify the weakness in existing system,
✓ Provide suggestions to the management on timely basis,
✓ Plan the timing of his further audit procedures **  |


### Factors that affect the judgment of the auditor regarding the determination of nature, timing and extent (NTE) of audit procedures to be applied

a. The result of the procedures already applied
b. The response of enquiries regarding operating effectiveness of internal control system.
c. The remaining audit period.
d. The volume of transactions remaining.
e. The evaluation of control environment of the entity.

## 9.5 TOOLS TO REVIEW INTERNAL CONTROL SYSTEM (220)

![img-3.jpeg](assets/audit%20book%20ch8,9_img-3.jpeg)



![[2fcdcd0e-33.png]]

https://youtu.be/bea_M4AW6Xs?t=5475&si=AQKhoVjx1d1UPveP
### 1. Narrative record
https://youtu.be/bea_M4AW6Xs?t=5485&si=ZMDTy-oZmwySYdz5

$\Rightarrow$ This record is written form of processes and flows of entity's rules and regulations (controls) in existence.
$\Rightarrow$ The auditor observes the entire system closely and makes a description of significant areas, nature of controls and the operating effectiveness of such controls.

**Benefits:**
- ☑ Simple and easy to understand.
- ☑ Suitable for smaller entities.
- ☑ Provides a useful supplement to flowcharting documentation

**Limitations:**
- ☑ They can be lengthy and difficult to review.
- ☑ Time consuming process.
- ☑ Weakness in the system cannot be easily located.
- ☑ Needs constant updation in case of versatile business environment.



### 2. Check-list 
https://youtu.be/bea_M4AW6Xs?t=5585&si=uvWNN_C-EsV3dyfC

It consists of series of questions prepared by the auditor and to be answered by the audit staff.
Auditor based upon his understanding and experience identifies the essential areas to be assessed upon and prepares the list of questions and asks the audit staff to enquire and answer.
Answers are generally in the format of “Yes”, “No”, “Not Applicable”
“Yes” answer denotes satisfactory position and a ‘No’ answer suggests weakness.

**Benefits :**
☑ There is less chance of overlooking the important areas.
☑ Audit staff can interact with the management directly.
☑ Weak areas can be located based upon enquires made.
☑ Evaluation can be made in easier manner.

**Limitations:**
☑ Client may not answer appropriately to the audit staffs.
☑ It requires detailed understanding and experience to prepare the checklist.

Refer the checklist in Illustration A.  


### 3. Internal Control Questionnaires 
 https://youtu.be/bea_M4AW6Xs?t=5649&si=3RJo2gyXnTP2kgcU
 
It is a set of questions relating to various aspects of the entity which are in one way or the other related to financial transactions.
The questions may relate to specific areas such as cash, fixed assets, sales etc.
It helps to analyze the operating effectiveness of the internal control system i.e. whether or not internal control system is able to prevent, detect or correct the misstatements on timely basis.

**Benefits :**
☑ It helps the auditor to identify weak areas.
☑ Based upon the results of evaluation, auditor determines the timing of further tests to be conducted.
☑ It help management and internal auditors document processes and highlight control gaps, strengths, and weaknesses within a system

**Limitations :**
☑ Requires overall understanding of the entity to prepare the questionnaire.
☑ Time consuming process.
☑ The questions which are not applicable to the entity, may be create a sense of wasteful time.  |


### 4. Flow Chart
https://youtu.be/bea_M4AW6Xs?t=5550&si=3vk0we302rL0o-Lu

- It is a graphic presentation of internal controls in the organization which provides concise and comprehensive way for reviewing the internal controls.
- The documents and activities are shown to flow horizontally from section to section.
- Concerned sections are shown as vertical column.
- Flow chart may be used for sales, purchase, wages, production etc.
- The main output of a flowchart is a process map — a graphical representation of events performed by a group of people.

**A properly drawn flowchart can show:**

a. at what point a document is raised internally or received from external sources;
b. the number of copies in which a document is raised or received
c. the intermediate stages through which document or activity passes
d. distribution of the documents to various sections, departments or operations,
e. checking authorization and matching at relevant stages
f. filing of documents and
g. final disposal by sending out or destruction.

**Benefits:**
- ☑ Concise presentation
- ☑ Easy understanding of overall system
- ☑ This chart can be introduced by audit managers as a control device for their audit operation

**Limitations:**
- ☑ Weakness in internal control system cannot be located easily
- ☑ Time consuming process
- ☑ Requires technical expertise to prepare flow chart.
