Before incorporation and commencement of business, company and the promoters of the company may incurred so many types of expenses like statuary fees, company logo designing, legal registration, feasibility study etc. The benefit of the preliminary expenses is long-term so it is treated as intangible asset and shown in Balance sheet under Miscellaneous assets and written off to profit and loss account over the period of time. The auditor shall consider the following:
	a. Check the bills and invoices relating to incorporation expenses
	b. Check the receipt issued by the concerned party for receiving the payment.
	c. Examine the resolution of the board and the power in Articles of Association (AOA) for reimbursement of such expenses to the promoters.
	d. Ensure that only those expenses that relate to the incorporation of the company are included.
	e. Ensure that after approval, these expenses are correctly accounted.  



**Sales Commission** 
Sales commission may be paid to the agents for selling the products of the entity. The commission is paid on the basis of agreement made between the entity and the agents. Such agreement is usually made for promoting the sales.
The auditor shall consider the following:
a. Check the agreement made with the agents.
b. Obtain an understanding of rate of commission to be paid
c. Examine the sales report sent by the agent and confirm with the statements of goods sent to agent.
d. Verify the mode of payment i.e. cash or bank.
e. Trace the entry in commission account
f. Ensure the correct accounting for these expenses.  



**Payment for Personal Expenses of directors** 
The personal expenses of the director are the facilities of his accommodation, transportation, entertainment etc. Those expenses are generally incurred as the facility provided to the director as a part of his remuneration for the services provided to the company.
The auditor shall consider the following:
	a. Obtain an understanding regarding the director’s remuneration and facilities from AOA and MOA
	b. Check the board’s minute books containing the resolution approving the personal expenses of the directors.
	c. Check the documentary evidences in support of the expenses reimbursed
	d. Ensure that no such expenses which are not made in connection with the company are accounted
	e. Ensure the compliance with the provisions of Income Tax Act. 2058 for incorporating the payments as a part of employment and withhold tax.  




**Remuneration paid to directors**
a. Examine the resolution of the general meeting or the board meeting for the criteria determined for remuneration to the directors.
b. Examine the AOA and resolution to determine the mode of payment to the directors (i.e monthly/ quarterly etc)
c. Verify the attendance of director in the meetings.
d. Trace the entry of payment in cash/ bank account.
e. Examine the receipt issued by the directors.
f. Ensure the compliance with Income Tax Act for withholding tax.  



**Payment of Income Tax** 
Income tax is paid on the taxable income calculated as per the Income Tax Act. For the payment of the Income Tax, the auditor shall consider the following:
a. The accuracy of calculation of taxable income should be checked
b. Ensure that the taxable income is computed by complying with the relevant provisions of Income Tax Act.
c. Ensure that the payment to revenue has been made on timely basis.
d. Trace the payment of taxes in the bank account.
e. Ensure the compliance with NAS on Income Taxes.
f. Ensure that the taxes have been deposited in the correct name and in correct heading.  


**Payment of Dividend** 
A dividend is a distribution of a portion of a company’s earnings, decided by the board of directors, to a class of its shareholders. It is a sum of money paid regularly (generally annually) by a company to its shareholders out of its profits (or reserves).
The auditor shall consider the following:
	a. Examine the provisions in AOA & MOA for the payment of dividends.
	b. For declaration of dividends, ensure that the provisions of AOA & MOA are properly complied with.
	c. Examine the minutes of the general meetings regarding the payment of dividend
	d. Verify the shareholders register and ensure that the names of all the shareholders who are entitled to receive the dividend are included.
	e. Check the computation of dividends with reference to rate of dividends and number of shares held by the shareholder.
	f. Examine the counterfoils of cheques for the amounts paid to shareholders.  




**Custom and Excise Duties**
Custom duties are generally paid through clearing agents.
	a. Verify the bill of entry (pragyapan patra) to ascertain the goods.
	b. Vouch the payments on the basis of challan/ receipt
	c. Examine the clearing agent's bill
	d. Verify the accounting for VAT and other charges.
	e. Trace the payment made (i.e. in cash or bank account)
	In the event of dispute, where the provisional payment has been made, the amount determined as payable finally should be ascertained and any additional duty payable or refund should be properly accounted.

Excise Duty is levied on manufacture. An excise is considered an indirect tax, meaning that the producer or seller who pays the tax to the government is expected to try to recover or shift the tax by raising the price paid by the buyer. Normally excise duty is paid before the issue of excisable goods from the factory.
The auditor shall consider the following:
	a. Check the details of goods produced
	b. Verify the accuracy of calculation of excise with respect to applicable rates.
	c. Cross verify with the payment schedule and issue permits for the goods.
	d. Examine the receipt (copy of challan) on payment of duty.
	e. Ensure that excise duty is correctly deducted from sales and accounted in trading account.



**Advance given to suppliers**
Advance given to the suppliers is the amount paid to suppliers in connection for the supply of goods to the entity. It is a normal business activity to pay the advance amount to suppliers. However, the advance payment should be suitably adjusted against the final payment.
The auditor shall consider the following:
	a. Obtain the list of suppliers to whom the advance payment has been made.
	b. For the recent payments, verify from the bank/cash accounts
	c. Check the receipt issued for acknowledgement of sum received.
	d. Conduct an aging analysis of the advances to confirm the balances are regular and moving (i.e. not idle)
	e. For the balances that are outstanding for a long period of time, ensure that management has initiated the reasonable steps for its recovery or settlement.
	f. For doubtful balances, ensure that appropriate provision has been made.
	g. For material amounts, obtain the external confirmations.



**Interest Expenses** 
Interest expenses are in the nature of borrowing costs. Simply, interest expense is charge paid for utilizing the funds.
The auditor shall consider the following:
a. Obtain the schedule of borrowings of the entity.
b. Obtain an understanding with regards to nature of loan, payment, rate of interest, period of repayment, break up to EMI etc.
c. Ensure that the calculation of interest is appropriate
d. Trace the amount of interest paid in bank statement.
e. Check the bank reconciliations for any differences in ledger balances.  



**Petty Cash Expenses** 
a. Identify the authority for handling the petty cash
b. Identify the limit for Imprest System
c. Ensure that internal controls over petty cash are appropriate.
d. Verify the cash book for transfer if cash under Imprest system.
e. Scrutinize petty vouchers along with invoices, bills and receipts.
f. Conduct a surprise check of petty cash balances and compare the same with petty cash book. 


**Other Revenue Expense (Electricity, Telephone, Water, Printing and stationary, General office expenses etc.** 
a. Check the invoices
b. Verify the mode of payment
c. Ensure correct accounting and disclosure
d. Trace the payment entries
e. Check receipts issued by the receiving party.  |

## 13.5 AUDIT OF RECEIPTS

The receipts of the entity may be in different forms such as revenue receipts which are generally the form of sale of goods and services; and the receipts may be from the disposal of capital assets at all.

For the audit of receipts, the basic points to be considered by the auditor are:

- Internal controls over receipts
- Documents and records that verify the accuracy of receipts
- The sales ledger verification
- Cash/ Bank Ledger verification
- Correctness of accounting


Some of the receipt transactions and the basic vouching points are mentioned below:


**Cash Sales** 
→ Cash sales forms important part of business activity because the settlement of transaction is made promptly when the customer pays the cash for the goods bought.
→ The Auditor has to consider the following
	a. Examine the internal control over receipts from sales.
	b. Ensure that there is an appropriate segregation of duties for making cash sales & receiving amount there from.
	c. Check the few bills for ascertaining accuracy of rate, amount, discount & Sales Tax/VAT etc.
	d. In case a large number of cash sales are affected, check cash sales summary book maintained by the client.
	e. Trace the relevant entry in cash book with reference to date on cash memos.
	f. For proper cash control, ensure that the cash collected in deposited into bank account subsequently.
	g. Trace the cash deposit entry in bank account
	h. Ensure that revenue has been recognized as per requirements of NAS- 07 “Revenue Recognition”.
	i. Ensure that the proper cut-off procedures are applied for the sales near the balance sheet date.  



**Credit Sales** 
→ The entity may have credit sales policy to increase its revenue.
→ Credit sale is a normal business activity whereby the customer is given a credit period to make the payment for the goods purchased by him.
	a. Auditor should obtain an understanding of credit sales policy and credit period allowed
	b. Ensure that the credit sales have been authorized by the competent authority.
	c. Verify the nature of goods to ensure that goods are those which are normally dealt in by client
	d. Examine copies of sales invoices issued to the customer
	e. Ensure that proper cut off procedures are applied.
	f. Check the customer ledger to cross verify the amount of invoice.
	g. For Material amounts, obtain the external confirmation.  



**Goods sent on Sale or Return basis** 
• Entity may provide the facility to its customers that goods are delivered to the customers with the option to retain or return the same within a specified short period.
• When the entity sends goods with such an option it is generally called “Sale or Return”. Such transaction cannot be treated as sales.
• Delivery of goods on approval basis implies a change of possession only and not a transfer of ownership unless the specified period expires without return or the customer earlier informs of his approval.
	a. The auditor should check whether a separate Memorandum record of goods sent out on sale or return basis has been maintained.
	b. Ensure that the on the receipt of acceptance from the party, the account has been debited and the sales has been accounted.
	c. Check that the provision for sales returns has been made against all the transactions for which the customer has the option to return the goods as on balance sheet date.
	d. The auditor should check that a provision for sales returns has been made against all the transactions for which the customer has the option to return the goods.
	e. All such goods should be included in closing stock.  



**Goods sent on consignment** 
• It is a trading arrangement in which a seller sends goods to a buyer or reseller who pays the seller only as and when the goods are sold.
• The seller remains the owner (title holder) of the goods until they are paid for in full and, after a certain period, takes back the unsold goods.
• It is also called sale or return, or goods on consignment.
• The person who consigns the goods is called “consignor” and the one to whom the goods are consigned is called “consignee.”
	a. Study the consignment agreement to identify the terms and conditions.
	b. Verify the entries in the consignment sale book with copies of invoices sent to consignee.
	c. Cross verify the proforma invoices and the account sales.
	d. Ensure that the difference between the cost & invoice price has been properly adjusted in accounts.
	e. Check whether commission due to consignee is as per the consignment agreements and such payment is made appropriately.
	f. Examine the copy of receipt for ensuring the payment made.
	g. Ensure that the goods in hand with the consignee is properly valued as per the proper valuation rule. (Generally cost + incurred expenses such as freight, custom due etc.)
	h. Ensure that proper allowance has been made for the damaged and obsolete items while making the valuation.
	i. Obtain confirmation from the consignee.  





**Sales Return** 
Sometimes the goods sold by the entity are returned back due to a defect in goods, excess supply of goods than ordered or similar reasons. In this case, the auditor has to consider the following:
	a. Examine sales return book with reference to copies of credit notes issued to customers and inward return notes
	b. Cross examine the debit note.
	c. Identify the cause of return by examining the correspondence with the customer.
	d. Examine Return inward register and Stores records
	e. Examine corresponding entry for return of goods in customer’s account.  



**Recovery of Bad debts written off** 
⇒ Sometimes, the entity has to write off its debtors for not being able to receive the due amount from them. The amount that is written off is treated as bad-debt.
⇒ However, such bad debts may be recovered later on, when the debtor settles his old dues.
⇒ The written off amount is treated as an expense being loss to the company. But on subsequent recovery, the amount has to be treated as income and properly accounted for.
	a. Obtain the list of bad debts appearing in client’s accounts.
	b. Examine that all recoveries against this have been shown in books
	c. Examine acknowledgement issued to debtors.
	d. Examine the notification from the court for bankruptcy of the party.
	e. Trace the entry of debtor which was written off as bad-debt.
	f. For the subsequent recovery, check the receipt issued to the debtor.
	g. Trace relevant entry in cash book.
	h. Ensure proper treatment in Profit and loss account as income.  


**Rent received** 
⇒ The entity may have an investment that generates rental revenue for e.g. the property sublet or leased by the entity.
⇒ Or, the entity may sublet its unused space to any party for generating the revenue in the form of rentals.
	a. Study the rent agreement to obtain an understanding of various term & conditions of agreements entered into with tenants.
	b. Obtain the list of properties let out
	c. Check copy of receipts issued to tenant to ensure that calculation of rent has been made as per terms
	(i.e. to ensure arithmetical accuracy)
	d. If the rent is collected by any agent, study the agreement with the agent to identify the terms and conditions of agency.
	e. For rent received in advance, ensure that the rent income is properly adjusted against advance amount.
	f. For the rent outstanding for a long period of time, enquire with the management.
	g. Ensure that the rent is properly booked and accounted.
	h. Obtain confirmation from tenants regarding amount paid by them
	i. Trace relevant entry in cash book or bank ledger for the rent received.
	j. Ensure that the rent has been booked at gross value and the TDS been properly adjusted.  



**Receipt of Capital Subsidy** 
Capital subsidy is a benefit given by the government (or any donor) to the entity usually in the form of a cash payment or similar arrangements for financing a capital asset.
a. Study the application made by the client for the claim of subsidy.
b. Study the sanction letter and the documents for the grant of the subsidy, to understand the terms and conditions.
c. Trace the entry in bank account for receipt of subsidy.
d. Ensure that the client entity has complied with the terms and conditions as mentioned in the sanction letter.
e. Check the accounting entries for the receipt of subsidy.
f. Examine the copy of receipt issued.
g. Ensure that the provisions of NAS-10 “Accounting for Government Grants and Disclosure of Government Assistance” are complied with.  



**Receipt of special backward area subsidy from Nepal Government** 
⇒ The subsidy received from Nepal Government may be in capital nature for funding the asset or a revenue nature for running the day to day operations.
⇒ If the grant is of capital nature for funding the asset, it may be:
✓ adjusted against the cost of asset or.
✓ it may be accounted as capital reserve and transferred to profit and loss account each year proportionately.
The auditor should check the compliance with NAS-10.
Other points are similar to Vouching of capital subsidy  


**Sale proceed of scrap material/ Junk material** 
The scrap or junk materials are those which are generated in the course of production and consumption. Unlike waste materials, these have monetary value.
The Auditor shall consider the following procedures:
	a. Determine the nature of industry and the scrap generation.
	b. Study and evaluate the internal control over generation, storage & disposal of junk material.
	c. Examine whether the entity has maintained reasonable records for the scrap materials.
	d. Review the production and cost records to identify the generation of scrap material at a particular period.
	e. Apply ARP’s to analyze the generation, sales revenue etc. for the two different periods.
	f. Check the rate at which different junk materials have been sold.
	g. Check the entry in cash/ bank ledger.
	h. Ensure that the sale proceeds are correctly accounted for.
	Note: As a matter of accounting policy, the sales of scrap can be shown as sales OR. Reduced from the cost of product.  



**Royalty Received** 
Royalty is a sum paid to a patentee for the use of a patent or to an author or composer for each copy of a book sold or for each public performance of a work.

a. Study the terms of contract between client (author) & the publisher.
b. For verifying the arithmetical accuracy, the periodical statements received from the publisher should be checked.
c. Verify the Bank/ Cash account to confirm receipts.
d. Check the acknowledgement issued to the payer.
e. For accrued royalty, ensure that the amount has been correctly accounted.  



**Commission received** 
Generally, Commission income refers to fees earned by brokers and agents in making a sale or closing a deal. It is the primary revenue account of real estate brokers, stock brokers, insurance agencies, etc.

However, entity may make commission income from referral services, unit sales etc.

The auditor has to consider the following points.
	a. Study the terms of contract with principal
	b. Check the arithmetical accuracy for the computation of commission by verifying with the terms and conditions of the agreement.
	c. Examine copy of receipts issued.
	d. Trace entry in cash book & relevant account
	e. Ensure that the tax implications are properly addressed.
	f. Ensure that the commission received is correctly accounted for.  


**Income from investment /interest & dividend** 
The entity make the investments in the form of:
	✓ Investment in Shares
	✓ Investment in Property or,
	✓ Investment in debentures or loans

The income from above may be vouched by considering the following:
	a. Study the AOA/MOA of the entity to identify the areas where the entity may make the investment.
	b. Examine the investment register to identify the nature of investment made by the entity
	c. Dividend may be vouched by the reference to counterfoils of dividend warrants.
	d. TDS certificates may be examined to cross verify the income.
	e. Ensure that Gross amount of interest /dividend has been properly reflected in Profit and Loss account.
	f. Verify whether the TDS deducted on gross value has been properly accounted.
	g. Trace the entry in cash/ bank account.  




**Sale of Investment** 
a. Examine the board minutes for the decision of the BOD to sell the investment.
b. Obtain an understanding how the investment was sold i.e. either through the broker or self
c. Check the nature of investment sold i.e. whether long term investment or short term investment.
d. If investment is sold through the broker, identify the brokerage or commission charges.
e. Ensure that the difference between the carrying amount and the sales proceeds, net of expenses, is recognized in the Profit & Loss Account.
f. Ensure that general principles of “Accounting for Investments” are complied with.  



**Insurance claims** 
As a matter of safeguard to assets or indemnification of loss from future contingent events, the entity might buy insurance plans for it’s various assets such as fixed assets or current assets.

When the asset’s are destroyed or there is loss of any kind, the entity can recover from the insurance company by making a claim.

The Insurance claim received must be suitably adjusted in the accounts.

The auditor shall consider the following:
	a. Identify the nature of asset for which the insurance claim is lodged.
	b. Examine the copy of insurance claim lodged with the insurance company.
	c. Cross examine the policy for identifying the validity of claim made.
	d. Check report of surveyor to ascertain the valuation of loss
	e. Check acknowledgement receipt issued to the insurance company
	f. Trace the relevant entry in cash/ bank account.
	g. Verify the receipts issued to insurer.
	h. If the amount received is less or more than the loss suffered, ensure that the loss or profit on claim has been suitably accounted in the profit and loss account.  


**Discounted bills receivable dishonored** 
A bill of exchange is said to be dishonoured when the drawee refuses to accept or make payment on the bill. A bill may be dishonored by non-acceptance or non-payment.
	☑ If the drawee refuses to accept the bill when it is presented before him for acceptance, it is called dishonor by non-acceptance. When a bill is dishonored by non-acceptance, an immediate right of recourse against the drawer and endorser accrues to the holder.
	☑ If the drawer has accepted the bill, but on the due date, he refuses to make payment of the bill, it is called dishonour by non-payment. In this case the holder has immediate right of recourse against each party to the bill.
The auditor shall consider the following:
	a. Obtain a schedule of discounted bills receivable dishonored.
	b. The amount collected in respect of bills receivable are verified by reference to Bills Receivable Book
	c. Check the entry in bank statement for the amount of bills dishonored and ensure that the bank has debited the account of the client.
	d. Verify the bills receivable returned by the bank along with the bank's advice.
	e. Check that the bank commission charged by the bank has been recovered from the party.  


**Package and Empties** 
☑ The packages, tins, boxes, bottles etc. are necessary for packaging goods.
☑ While selling such types of well packed goods, a provision could be made with the customers for the returns of such type of containers.
☑ At the time of issue, customer's account is debited with the cost of containers and credited when they are returned.
☑ If the customer returns the containers on time his account will be credited with the value less than the original cost of the container (for the purpose of maintaining depreciation.)
☑ Containers for which period specified for returning them has not expired, should be treated as stock with the customer and are carried forward to next accounting year at depreciated value along with stock in hand of containers.
☑ The auditor should see that a provision has been made for containers not returned by customers within time.  


**Sale of departmental stocks** 
☑ Review the procedure of sales recognition.
☑ Verify the actual sales with the recorded sales.
☑ Check the price of the sales and compare with the standard price.
☑ Examine the payment received through cash/ bank account.
☑ Verify the stock records.  |


## POSSIBLE REASONS FOR THE SHARP DECREASE IN THE RATE OF GROSS PROFIT ON SALES

1. Overvaluation of the opening stock.
2. Under valuation of closing stock.
3. Change in basis of valuation of closing stock. For example where the closing stock was valued at cost or market rate whichever was lower, valuing the opening stock at the market price which is higher than cost.
4. Amount of goods purchased in the previous year, which were physically received in this year, included in the purchases of current year.
5. Reversal of the fictitious sale entries recorded in the previous year to boost the profits.
6. Excessive provision made for wages and other direct expenses.
7. Failure to account for goods sold.
8. Failure to take credit for the amount of an insurance claim in respect of goods lost in transit or destroyed by the fire.

## POSSIBLE REASONS FOR THE SHARP INCREASE IN THE RATE OF GROSS PROFIT ON SALES

1. Undervaluation of opening stock.
2. Overvaluation of closing stock.
3. Change in the basis of valuation of closing stock. E.g. where the opening stock was valued at cost or market rate whichever was lower, valuing the closing stock at the market price which is higher than cost.
4. Inclusion of goods received on a consignment basis, in the closing stock.
5. Treatment of goods sent out for sale on consignment basis as regular basis i.e. after adding profit margin.
6. Wrong allocation of expenses e.g. freight inward may be wrongly taken to the profit and loss account.
7. No provision or under-provision in the expenses account included in the Trading Account.

## 13.6 VERIFICATION

The balance sheet of the entity shows the position of assets and liabilities as on the reporting date which is normally the end of financial year.

The auditor has to ensure that the assets and liabilities are properly reflected in the balance sheet. The process applied by the auditor to ensure the correctness of disclosure of assets and liabilities in the balance sheet is verification.

Verification is the act of assuring the correctness of value of assets and liabilities, title and their existence in the organization. An auditor should be satisfied himself about the actual existence of assets and liabilities appearing in the balance sheet is correct.


### Verification of Assets

The various assets as reflected in the balance sheet may be in the form of Fixed Assets, Investments and current assets that include inventories, debtors etc.

It is necessary to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the presentation of these assets because any undervaluation or overvaluation may lead to misstatements in the financial statements taken as a whole.

Primary responsibility of verification of assets is that of the management. It is because no other person other than the management of the entity has a true knowledge about the condition of their assets.

However, the auditor is required to verify the original cost of assets and to confirm, as far as practicable, that such a valuation is fair and reasonable.

*Assets are valued either on a ‘going concern’ or a ‘break-up value’ basis. ‘Going Concern’ basis is considered appropriate when the entity is operating appropriately in the normal course of the business and the “Break-up value” basis is considered, when the business has closed down and is being wound-up. Assets may be Tangible or Intangible Assets.*

Common examples are:

| Tangible Assets                                                                                                             | Intangible Assets                                                                                                                                          |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| ☑ Land<br>☑ Buildings<br>☑ Plant and Equipment<br>☑ Furniture and fixtures<br>☑ Vehicles<br>☑ Office Equipments<br>☑ Others | ☑ Goodwill<br>☑ Trade Marks<br>☑ Computer software<br>☑ Patents<br>☑ Copyrights<br>☑ Mortgage servicing rights,<br>☑ Fishing licenses<br>☑ Import quotas   |





## 13.7 OBJECTIVE OF VERIFICATION

The objective of verification of assets is to identify the following:

|  1. Existence | ☑ that the assets were in existence on the date of the balance sheet  |
| --- | --- |
|  2. Authorization | ☑ that the asset is purchased under proper authority (i.e. compliance with control)  |
|  3. Cost | ☑ that all the costs relevant to assets are properly accounted for (i.e. capitalization)  |
|  4. Ownership | ☑ that the right of ownership of the assets vested in or belonged to the undertaking  |
|  5. Free from charges | ☑ that they were free from any lien or charge not disclosed in the balance sheet  |
|  6. Valuation | ☑ that they had been correctly valued having regard to their physical condition  |
|  7. Disclosure | ☑ that their values are correctly disclosed in the balance sheet  |



## 13.8 VALUATION OF ASSETS

→ Fixed assets are acquired with an objective of earning revenue and not for the purpose of sale. Almost all fixed assets except land suffer depletion or exhaustion due to efflux of time and their use or exploitation.

→ However in case of mines and quarries, i.e. the *wasting assets*, their value diminishes on exploitation, contrary to the loss of value through use or obsolescence that takes place in the case of other assets.

→ Floating assets such as stock in trade, book debts, bills receivable etc are acquired for resale with a view to earning profits or are those that come into existence during the processes of trade or manufacture.

The general principles for valuation of assets are mentioned below:

1. **Fixed Assets** 
→ Fixed assets are included in the Balance Sheet at their cost less depreciation and impairment loss.
→ In case if government grant is received in relation to specific fixed assets, then:
	✓ either the grant can be shown as deduction from cost of the asset OR
	✓ grant can be treated as deferred income which is recognized in Profit and Loss Account  


2. **Wasting Assets** 
→ Provision for depreciation or depletion should be on the basis of the estimated physical exhaustion that takes place.
→ Physical exhaustion can be estimated on the basis of expected output during the working life of wasting asset.  

3. **Floating assets** 
→ These are generally included in the Balance sheet at their realizable value.
→ Therefore, they are valued either at cost or market value whichever is less.  


## 13.9 VERIFICATION OF SPECIFIC ASSETS

Some general procedures for the verification of specific assets are mentioned below:

1. **Land and Building** 
	Land is non-depreciable asset whereas building is subject to depreciation. So it is recommended to show land and building separately in the balance sheet.
		a. Check casting and compare the opening balance brought forward from previous year.
		b. Obtain schedules of addition during the year.
		c. Test capital expenditure for authorization.
		d. Inspect the title deeds to confirm the ownership of the asset.
		e. If the property has been mortgaged, obtain MRL and confirmation for the same and ensure that mortgage is properly disclosed.
		f. Test check against the supplier’s invoices or other independent vouchers to ensure revenue and capital are properly distinguished.
		g. If the building is constructed using own labor check all the labor cost is properly accounted.
		h. Ensure that the building is depreciated properly. The provisions of Income Tax Act regarding depreciation should be complied with.  



2. **Assets Acquired on Hire Purchase** 
	a. Inspect hire-purchase agreement to obtain an understanding of the terms and conditions.
	b. Ensure that the assets acquired under hire purchase are treated as assets acquired under finance lease.
	c. If it is certain that ownership will be transferred to lessee at the end of the term, ensure that the asset is depreciated over it’s useful life OTHERWISE asset should be depreciated over the shorter of its useful life and the lease term.
	d. Ensure that it is shown separately in the Balance Sheet.  



3. **Lease hold property** 
	a. Terms and conditions of lease contract should be examined by checking the lease deed.
	b. If a part of the leasehold property has been sublet, examine the tenant’s agreements.
	c. Ensure that lease deed is complete in all respect.
	d. Verify relevant documents to check cost of property.
	e. Ensure that NAS on Accounting for lease has been followed.  




4. **Plant & Machinery** 
	a. Study the internal controls over the authorization and purchase of the plant and machinery.
	b. Ensure that the existence of the plant and machinery is in consonance with the objective of the entity.
	c. If new plant and machinery is acquired during the year, check the board minutes and decisions to validate the purchase of machinery.
	d. Examine whether installation costs and other charges incurred in this connection have been capitalized.
	e. Ensure that routine maintenance charges are debited to P&L Account.
	f. Auditor should examine the existence of charge by inspecting register of charges.
	g. Study the physical verification report of the management.
	h. Examine whether the profit or loss on disposal has been calculated and disclosed properly in the financial statements.
	i. Examine whether the provision for depreciation has been made in accounts at appropriate amounts.
	j. If the asset has been revalued during the financial year, obtain MRL and ensure that revaluation is appropriate.  



 5. **Furniture and Fixture** 
	Furniture constitute movable items such as desk, chair etc.
	Fixture is a type of furniture which is fixed in specific place and position of building. Fixtures are sold and transferred with the real property. For Eg: book cases, plumbing etc.
	While verifying the furniture and fixture, the auditor has to consider the following:
		a. Identify the nature of furniture that the entity owns.
		b. Enquire about the locations and conditions of the furniture and fixture.
		c. Conduct physical verification to ensure the existence of furniture and fixture.
		d. Examine the internal controls over the identification and custody of the furniture.
		e. Ensure that depreciation has been properly charged on the items as per acceptable & consistent policy.
		f. Ensure that the lost/damaged furniture and fittings have been written off in the profit and loss account.
		g. Ensure that all the items of furniture and fixture are properly disclosed and accounted for.  



6. **Motor Vehicles** 
	Entity may own vehicles for it's business purpose. These may be cars, bikes, delivery van etc. The auditor has to consider the following:
		a. Examine the authorization for purchase of vehicles.
		b. Examine the invoices for purchase of vehicles and ensure that all the costs have been properly capitalized.
		c. Examine insurance policies taken for vehicles. Insurance policy may be taken as third party insurance, theft insurance etc.
		d. Examine the vehicle registration documents issued by transport department.
		e. Check whether any charge has been created on motor vehicles, if so, ensure that it is properly disclosed.
		f. Ensure that the motor vehicles have been valued and disclosed at cost less depreciation.
		g. Cross check the arithmetical accuracy for depreciation computed
		h. Conduct physical verification for few items.  


7. **Investments** 
	As per the objectives, the entity may hold investments in its name. The investment may be in the form of marketable securities (short term investments) or long-term investments (held-to-maturity). It is matter of management decision to classify the investment as long term or short term.
		a. Obtain schedule of securities and shares in hand at beginning and at end of the period.
		b. Identify the date of purchase, face value, book value, rate of return, date of dividend (estimate etc.)
		c. Examine the broker's note, agreement etc. for purchase and sale of investments.
		d. Ensure that all the costs relating to investments are properly accounted and disclosed.
		e. Pay special attention to the purchase and sale of investments cum-dividend, ex-dividend etc.
		f. Obtain schedule of securities and shares purchased and sold during the year.
		g. In case, investments are in physical form, inspect the investment certificates at the end of the accounting period.
		h. For the investments that are kept in DMAT form, obtain statement from depository.
		i. Ensure that the current & long term investments have been properly classified.
		j. Ensure that the valuation of investment as per their classification is correct.  



8. **Inventories** 
	Inventories refer to the raw materials, work-in-process goods and finished goods that are considered to be the portion of a business's assets that are ready or will be ready for sale.
	Inventory form the most important part of current assets because the turnover of inventory represents one of the primary sources of revenue generation.
		a. Obtain an understanding of effectiveness of internal controls for stock movement.
		b. Examine various stock records like receiving reports, inspection reports, material issue notes etc.
		c. Ensure that management has made proper routine for physical verification of inventories
		d. Attend & observe physical count of inventory conducted by the management.
		e. Enquire whether if any charges are created on inventory.
		f. Ensure that a proper cut-off procedure has been followed.
		g. Perform Analytical Review Procedure to identify the variation in stock movement.
		h. Ensure the compliance with NAS -04 regarding valuation and disclosure of inventories.  



 9. **Capital work in progress** 
	Capital work in progress refers to the asset that is under construction and has not been completed till the date of Balance-Sheet.
	Capital work in progress may be plant and machinery under construction, building under construction etc.
	Capital work in progress account contains all expenses incurred on the asset until it is converted into working condition.
	Verify the nature of investment in asset and ensure that the capital project is authorized by the board.
		a. The auditor has to carefully assess the stage of completion of the work-in-progress for assessing the appropriateness of its valuation.
		b. Ascertain that the costs are properly allocated for work in progress.
		c. Test the correctness of the cost as disclosed by the cost records by verification of quantities and cost of materials, wages and other charges included in the cost sheets.
		d. Verify the invoices for the ascertaining the purchase cost of plant and machinery or building purchased.
		e. Ensure that the completed assets are not classified as work in progress and are properly reflected in depreciation schedule.
		f. Enquire with the engineers and other authorities for confirming the value of WIP. (obtain certificates)  



10. **Bank Balances** 
	a. Obtain the list of bank accounts maintained by the entity.
	b. Compare the entries in ledger of the client with entries in cash book/ bank statement.
	c. Examine fixed deposit receipts and bank advices for verification of fixed deposits made.
	d. Cash in transit should be verified with reference to their subsequent credit in bank account.
	e. Examine the bank reconciliation statement to ascertain the differences.
	f. Enquire about those items in reconciliation statement which are outstanding for a long period of time. Ensure whether any adjustment for such items is required.
	g. Obtain certificate from the bank regarding the balance confirmation.  



11. **Cash in Hand** 
	a. Obtain an understanding about the internal controls over cash handling.
	b. Determine the allocation of petty cash by the appropriate authority.
	c. Check the cash ledger account to identify any period which shows negative cash balance.
	d. Conduct surprise check for the verification of cash balances.
	e. Examine all items of cash balance e.g. Main cash, petty cash, imprest balances with the employees etc. simultaneously.
	The auditor should advise the entity to follow the practice of depositing the cash receipts to bank immediately so that the chance of loss or misappropriation in reduced.  



12. **Assets Abroad** 
	Sometimes, the entity may have some assets outside the country. Such assets may be in the form of foreign investments, land and property acquired abroad in the entity's name etc. In such case the auditor should consider the following:
		a. Obtain the list of such properties held by the entity.
		b. Ensure that the acquisition of the property is within the objective of the company.
		c. Examine the title deeds relating to such property.
		d. Verify the costs associated with such property by inspecting the invoices and related documents.
		e. Ensure that all such properties are properly disclosed by the management.
		f. Obtain MRI, from the management, regarding their responsibility to disclose the assets at fair value.
		g. If the assets are being held by any third party, auditor should obtain the certificate from such party confirming the existence of such assets.  



13. Stock lying with the third party. 
Some time, the stock of the auditee entity may be held by third parties in normal course of business for various reasons such as safe custody, sale on approval where approval is pending etc.
a. Obtain MRL as regards to reasons of stock lying with third parties.
b. Obtain external confirmation from the party that holds the stock.
c. Ensure about the condition of the stock lying with third party.
d. For any loss reported, ensure that the entity has made appropriate provision.
e. Ensure that the goods have been included in the closing stock at the end of reporting period  



14. **Prepaid Expenses** 
	Prepaid expenses refer to those expenses paid in advance but which has not yet been incurred. As per the accrual system of accounting, expense must be recorded in the accounting period in which it is incurred.
	Therefore, prepaid expense must be shown as asset at first and subsequently transferred to expense in the subsequent accounting periods in which the services in respect of the prepaid expense have been performed.
		a. Examine the supporting to verify the prepaid expenses.
		b. Check the bank/ cash ledger to trace the payment.
		c. Verify the nature of expense
		d. Ensure that all the prepaid expenses are properly disclosed in the balance sheet under the head current assets.  


15. **Small Tools/ Loose Tools** 
	These are the tools used in manufacturing operations that are below the corporate capitalization limit. Simply, the tools that are used for internal purpose (self-consumption) are known as small tools. For example: Hammers, Pliers, Screwdrivers, and Wrenches etc.
		a. Auditor shall obtain an understanding of the management policy regarding the small tools.
		b. Identify the internal controls over authorization of small tools purchase, manufacture and custody of these tools.
		c. Examine the production records and production order to find out the quantities and types of tools manufactured.
		d. Obtain the list of inventory of tools as well as details of date of acquisition, copy of invoice etc.
		e. Examine whether there is proper internal control over its issuance and storage.
		f. Ensure the consistency for the method of valuation adopted for small tools.
		g. If there is change in method of valuation, it should be disclosed in the financial statements.
		h. Ensure that the inventory does not include any worn out or defective article, whose life has already exhausted.
		i. For the year end valuation, ensure that these are valued at lower of cost or market price.  



| 16. Patents |     |
| ----------- | --- |
|             |     |


17. Copyrights
	Copyright is a form of protection provided to the authors of original works of authorship which includes literary, dramatic, musical, artistic, and certain other intellectual works, which may be published or unpublished.
		a. The auditor should obtain a schedule of copyrights from client.
		b. Ensure that all the costs relating to purchase (where copyrights are purchased) are properly accounted.
		c. Check whether the renewal fees have been paid on due dates.
		d. Examine the renewal slip.
		e. Ensure that the valuation of copyrights is appropriately made. Generally, they are revalued at cost less amortization charges till date.
		f. Ensure that the cost of trademarks and copyright are amortized over the period of legal validity or useful commercial life, whichever is shorter.
		g. If the auditor finds that any publication has ceased to command sale, he should have the amount of its copyright written off to revenue  



18. **Trademarks / Service marks** 
	A trademark is a word, name, symbol or device which is used in trade with goods to distinguish goods and enable their independent identity.
		a. Examine the legal documents and certificate of registration for trademarks.
		b. The auditor may seek legal advice, if there is any doubt over the custody of trademarks.
		c. Verify the agreement with the seller if the trademarks are purchased.
		d. Ensure that there is proper renewal of trademarks.
		e. Examine copy of receipt for renewal payments made.
		f. Ensure that trademarks are shown in the balance sheet at their cost less amortization charges.  



19. **Goodwill** 
	Goodwill is the monetary amount paid in excess of the value of net assets acquired while acquiring the business (i.e. business purchase). It is an intangible asset for the entity which has purchases the business.
	Self generated goodwill is ignored from the point of view of accounting.
		a. Study the business purchase agreement to determine the value of goodwill.
		b. Examine board authorization for purchase or rising of goodwill.
		c. Examine consistency of method of valuation of goodwill.
		d. Ensure that goodwill is appropriately written off over it's estimated useful life.
		e. Ensure that there is adequate disclosure of goodwill in the balance sheet.  


20. **Debtors** 
	A debtor is a person or entity that owes money. In other words, the debtor has a debt or legal obligation to pay an amount to another person or entity. Debtors are also the part of current assets. Study the sales policy of the entity regarding the credit sales and recovery.
		a. Examine the debtor records as maintained by the entity.
		b. Examine the copies of invoice with the customer accounts.
		c. Ensure whether the balances shown in the ledger accounts are consistent with balances as per control accounts.
		d. Verify whether the entity has classified the debtors as per their time of occurrence (i.e. aging of debtors).
		e. For the bad debts, ensure that the provision has been made after proper follow up and management authorization.
		f. Examine the correspondence made with the debtors for claiming the dues.
		g. For material amounts, obtain external confirmations directly from the debtors.
		h. Perform Analytical Review Procedures to make a comparison and analysis of various ratios and trends relating to debtors. For example: debtors turnover ratio, aging schedule analysis etc.
		i. Ensure that all the debtors are properly reflected in the balance sheet.  




21. **Bills Receivables** 
	Bill receivables are those bills whose amount will be received on due date from debtor or the person whose name in it as drawee. Examine whether the opening balance of bills receivable are correctly brought forward.
		a. Where the bills have been matured but the amount in respect thereof has not been received, ensure that these have been renewed subsequently.
		b. Enquire regarding the long outstanding or overdue bills.
		c. Obtain a confirmation certificate from the bankers for bills held by them for collection.
		d. Ensure that the provision has been made for dishonored bills.
		e. Ensure that all the receivables are properly shown in the Balance Sheet.  



22. **Sinking Fund policies/Endowment Policies** 
	A sinking fund is a fund established by an entity by setting aside revenue over a period of time to fund a future capital expense, or repayment of a long-term debt such as redemption of debenture.
		a. Inspect the policy to identify the nature and purpose of the policy.
		b. Ensure that the policy taken doesn’t violate the provisions stated in the objectives of the company.
		c. Ascertain the amount of premium payable.
		d. Ensure that the entity has complied with the provisions of the policy agreement.
		e. Ensure that value of the policy has been properly disclosed in the Financial Statements.  


  23. **Contingent Assets** 
	Contingent assets are those assets in which the possibility of an economic benefit depends solely upon future uncertain events. These are not recorded in the balance sheet as it would amount to taking credit for the revenue which has not accrued.
	Although there is no obligation to disclose the contingent assets in the financial statements, it is recommended to disclose the material contingent assets in a note.
		a. Obtain an understanding of the nature if probable economic benefit.
		b. Review any developments whether the realization is certain.
		c. Ensure that these are not accounted in the financial statements.  



## 13.10 VERIFICATION OF LIABILITIES

Liability is defined as an obligation borne by the entity during the normal course of business. It is an obligation that is reported on a company’s balance sheet. Examples of liabilities are loans payable, accounts payable, accrued expenses, wages payable, and taxes.

Current Liabilities are those which are expected to be settled within one year and all other liabilities other than the current liabilities are referred as Long-term liabilities.

Understatement or overstatement of liability leads to misstatement in the financial statements, therefore it is necessary verify the position of liabilities to ensure that the financial statements give a True and Fair view with regards to liabilities as well.



### Vouching And Verification

General procedures to verify the liability are:

☑ Examination of records
☑ Confirmation from lenders/suppliers
☑ Examination of disclosure
☑ Analytical Review Procedures
☑ Obtaining management representations

Verification of specific liabilities:

 1. **Loans and Borrowings** 
	The entity may borrow sums from lenders (banks or individuals) for meeting its day to day fund requirements.
	From financial leverage point of view, the entity also considers debt equity ratio when it borrows the funds. The auditor shall consider the following for verifying the loans and borrowings:
		a. Study the provisions mentioned in the MOA and AOA to determine the borrowing powers of the company.
		b. Ensure that the shareholders have ratified in cases the directors have exceeded their borrowing powers.
		c. For secured loans, identify the security pledged by the entity and obtain MRL from the management regarding the disclosure of the charge.
		d. Ensure that the borrowings have been utilized for the entity's purpose.
		e. Obtain confirmations and certificates from the lenders to confirm the amount of borrowings disclosed by the entity.
		f. Ensure the compliance.  



 2. **Contingent Liability** 
	Contingent liability refers to an obligation arising from the past events or circumstances that will be known only on happening or non-happening some future uncertain event.
	Obtain MRL containing a statement of contingent liabilities.
	The examples of contingent liabilities include warranty claims, litigation involving moral pressure by the management etc.
		a. Inspect the minute books and board decisions to ascertain the possibility of contingent liabilities.
		b. Examine the bills issued by the lawyers and legal consultants to identify whether they are related to any litigations and claims.
		c. Obtain an understanding of the pending legal cases and discuss with management and lawyer.
		d. If the liability is certain or is estimated to be certain, an appropriate provision should be made. Therefore, the auditor should ensure that such items are not included in contingent liability.
		e. Examine the bank letters to ascertain the guarantees on behalf of other companies or individuals.
		f. Obtain MRL that all the known contingent liabilities have been disclosed to the auditor.
		g. Ensure the compliance with NAS "Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets."  



  3. **Bills Payable** 
	A bill payable is a document which shows the amount owed for goods or services received on credit.
		a. Obtain an understanding of the internal control procedures for acceptance of bills.
		b. Obtain a schedule of bills containing details of terms, conditions etc and vouch the payments made to retire the bills on their maturity.
		c. Trace the entries in bills payable book to ensure arithmetical accuracy and appropriate disclosure.
		d. Obtain confirmation from drawers of bills payable regarding amounts due thereon.
		e. Reconcile the total of bills payable outstanding at the end of the year with the balance in bills payable account.
		f. Examine appropriateness and disclosure of the charge, if any, created on any asset for the payment of bills.  



  4. **Trade Creditors** 
	A creditor is an entity, a company or a person of a legal nature that has provided goods, services or a monetary loan to a debtor.
	Simply, creditor refers to the supplier of goods or services to the auditee entity.
		a. Obtain an understanding of the entity's credit policy, suppliers and nature of supplies that are obtained in credit.
		b. Study the schedule of creditors as reflected in balance sheet and examine it with individual creditor's accounts.
		c. Examine the purchase ledger and cross verify with the purchase invoices.
		d. Identify the criteria for discount on creditors.
		e. Check the stock ledger account to confirm the receipt of the good.
		f. Examine goods inward book to check that all the goods received near the balance sheet date have been duly accounted for.
		g. Perform Analytical Procedure to analyze the credit occurrence and variability of credits.
		h. Enquire with the management regarding long outstanding creditors.
		i. Select few material creditors and obtain direct confirmations.  


  5. **Amount due to subsidiary companies** 
	a. Study the MOA to confirm whether the subsidiary company is authorized to advance loans to the holding company.
	b. Identify the various terms and conditions regarding the rate of interest, due date of payment etc.
	c. Verify whether the terms of loan are reasonable as compared to the market trend.
	d. Cross examine the balance sheet of subsidiary company to ensure that the amount has been properly reflected in the balance sheet of the subsidiary company.
	e. Ensure the compliance of NAS on "Related Party Transactions".  



  6. **Outstanding Expenses** 
	Outstanding expenses refer to those expenses which have been incurred and consumed during an accounting period and are due to be paid, but are not paid.
	Examples include outstanding salary, outstanding rent, etc.
	Outstanding expenses are recorded in the books at the end of an accounting period to show true position of expenses incurred during the period and liability borne.
		a. Obtain a list of outstanding expenses as on the balance sheet date.
		b. Perform Analytical Review Procedures to understand the variation in liability and expenses as compared to the previous period.
		c. Ensure that all usual outstanding expenses like salaries, wages, rent etc have been provided.
		d. Verify the documentary evidence supporting the outstanding expenses.
		e. Ensure that the outstanding expenses have been shown as Current Liabilities in Balance Sheet and all the expenses have been properly disclosed.  



  7. **Provisions** 
An amount from profits that has been put aside in a company's accounts to cover a future liability is called a provision. The main purpose to provide provision is to allow a current year's balance to become more accurate.
A provision is recorded in a liability account, which is typically classified on the balance sheet as a current liability.
Example: Provision for income tax, provision for bonus, provision for bad-debts etc.

Provision for Tax
	a. Check the calculation of assessable income as per Income Tax Act.
	b. For completed assessments under income tax act, ensure that the adjustments have been properly made.
	c. For previous years provisions, ensure that the actual liability has been properly adjusted and accounted.
	d. If the appropriate provision has not been made, that would lead to material misstatement, auditor should qualify his report.

Provision for Bonus
	a. Ensure the arithmetical accuracy of computation of bonus.
	b. Ensure the compliances with Bonus Act, 2030 regarding the criteria for payment of bonus, deposit to welfare fund etc.
	c. Ensure proper disclosure of the provision for bonus.  


## Questions

1. Differentiate between vouching and verification.

**Answer:**

|  Particulars | Vouching | Verification  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  1. Meaning | Vouching means the examination of documentary evidence in support of transactions contained in the books of account. | Verification refers to examination whether assets and liabilities are properly stated in the Balance Sheet.  |
|  2. Objective | To establish authenticity of the transactions recorded in the primary books of accounts. | To inquire and confirm the ownership, valuation, existence and presentation of assets and liabilities.  |
|  3. Authority | Generally vouching is conducted by junior staff. | Verification is conducted by senior staff.  |
|  4. Time period | Vouching is generally conducted the year around. | It is conducted at the year end.  |
|  5. Basis | Mostly documentary evidences are checked. | It constitutes both documentary evidences and observation  |



2. Assets purchased under Hire-Purchase System were reflected at their full value and the outstanding installments payable have been included under Sundry Creditors. How will you deal with the above situation? (ICAI)

**Answer:**

|  Accounting Treatment | For assets acquired under HP System, the capital portion of the installments paid up to date of Balance Sheet should be debited to the Assets Account, and the Interest included in each installment and penal interest, if any, and should be charged off to revenue.  |
| --- | --- |
|  Depreciation | Depreciation should be provided on the full Cash Purchase Price of the asset. The Book Value should be shown in the Balance Sheet.  |
|  Conclusion | The treatment given by the Company in the accounts is not correct and shall be rectified in the above manner.  |

3. No depreciation has been charged for the year ended 31st Asar in respect of a Spare Bus purchased during the year and kept ready by the Company for use as a stand-by on the ground that it was not used during the year. Comment on the Auditor's duty.

4. A Company has not provided depreciation on Machinery on the plea that the Machinery has been maintained in excellent condition and is as good as new. Comment.

**Hints:**

Depreciation is a measure of the wearing out, consumption or other loss of value of depreciable asset arising from use, efflux of time or obsolescence through technology and market changes.

Depreciation also arises due to the efflux of time and, therefore, should be provided irrespective of whether the assets were put to use at all during the year.



## 13.11 AUDIT OF LEDGERS

**Scrutiny of General Ledger** 
→ A general ledger is a complete record of financial transactions over the life of a company.
→ It holds account information that is needed to prepare financial statements, and includes accounts for assets, liabilities, owners' equity, revenues and expenses.
→ The general ledger consists those transactions which are ultimately included in the income statement and balance sheet.
→ Some general ledger accounts are summary records which are referred to as control accounts.
→ The detail that supports each of the control accounts will be found outside of the general ledger in what is known as a subsidiary ledger.
→ The balances in the general ledger should be traced to the trial balance and ultimately financial statements.
→ Scrutiny of general ledger is done to ensure that the balances reflected in final accounts are correct and appropriately transferred.
→ The Auditor should also ensure that the balances reflected are in tune with the applicable accounting practices and the fundamental accounting principles are not violated.  



**Audit Of Impersonal Ledger** 
Impersonal accounts refer to real accounts and nominal accounts.
**Real accounts**
	→ It consists of the balance sheet accounts such as the accounts for recording assets, liabilities, and the owner's (or stockholders') equity.
**Nominal accounts**
	→ It consists of the income statement accounts such as the accounts for recording revenues, expenses, gains, and losses.
	→ The following points are considered for the audit of impersonal ledgers.
		✓ Cash transactions are to be checked on the basis of cash book or journal.
		✓ An auditor has to check whether there is a sufficient appropriate evidence for the recorded transactions.
		✓ Special attention should be given while checking transfer entries as it may affect final accounts.
		✓ Totals and balances of impersonal ledger should be verified with the balance shown in trial balance.
		✓ Opening balance of impersonal ledger should be verified with the audited account of previous year.
		✓ Auditor should thoroughly check the totals of the various other books of original entry and also the postings of their totals of the impersonal ledger.  




**Self Balancing Ledgers** 
	→ Self-balancing system is a system whereby separate Trial Balance can be taken out from each ledger.
	→ “General Ledger Adjustment Account” will be maintained in each of the sales and bought ledger.
	→ It has the following characteristics:
		a. Control accounts are prepared in all the ledgers. In the general ledger, debtor’s ledger adjustment account and creditor’s ledger adjustment account are prepared.
		b. A trial balance can independently be prepared from each one of the ledgers.
		c. All the ledgers form part of double entry system.  



**Sectional Balancing Ledgers** 
	→ Under sectional balancing system two accounts are maintained in the General ledger. They are:
		a. Total Debtors Account or Sales ledger Control Account
		b. Total Creditors Account or Purchase ledger Control Account
		It has the following characteristics:
		a. Double entry system is not applied
		b. Only control accounts are prepared in general ledger
		c. Trial balance may be prepared only in the general ledger  


**Loose leaf ledger** 
→ Each account is recorded in each loose leaf.
→ Each leaf is serially numbered.
→ Classification may be done alphabetically.
→ They are bounded together and kept safely.
→ Leaf can be added as required therefore separate ledger may not be required.  


**Card ledger** 
→ These ledgers are normally used in banks.
→ One account is kept in each card and it is printed in accounting machine. After giving serial numbers the cards are classified alphabetically.
→ These cards are kept separately so that any card can be sorted out as required.  


**Material Ledger Card** 
	→ These ledgers are used in a job order cost system to track and record the number of units that are purchased and issued to the production line.
	→ Simply, it is a manual record of the units of materials flowing.
	→ It contains the following information:
		✓ Purchases of raw materials
		✓ Transfers of raw materials to the production floor
		✓ Receipts back of unused items
		✓ Adjustments to on-hand balances based on the outcome of periodic inventory counts  



1. Write Short Notes on:

a. Control Accounts
- Control accounts are general ledger accounts as a part of double entry system that is used to summarize a large number of transactions.
- They help to ensure the accuracy of ledger accounts. They are mainly used with regard to receivables and payables balances.
- Control accounts are mainly used to help identify errors in the subsidiary ledgers, but the use of them gives a business a number of additional advantages.
- Control accounts allow a single trial balance to be extracted from the general ledger.
- If the trial balance does not balance, only the accounts whose control accounts does not reconcile need to be checked for errors.

Control accounts reduce the amount of detail needed in the general ledger.




# Chapter 14: AUDIT OF SPECIAL SECTORS

→ This chapter deals with basic guidelines for conducting the audit of various institutions such as Educational Institutions, Hospitals, Hotels, NGO's, Clubs, etc.

→ The Basic guidelines cover the major areas such as:
	A. Understanding the Entity and Planning Activities
	B. Audit Of Incomes/ Receipts
	C. Audit Of Expenses/ Payments
	D. Audit Of Assets
	E. Audit of Liabilities

## 14.1 AUDIT OF EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTION

Educational Institutions are those institutions which are engaged in the service of educational activities. Such Institutions may be in the nature of schools, colleges, coaching centers etc.

### A. Understanding the Entity and Planning Activities

| 1. AOA / MOA                             | → Study the AOA and MOA of the entity to identify the objectives, powers and governance structure.                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 2. Compliance with Acts                  | → Study the provisions of Education Act and Education Rules that are relevant to the entity and ensure their compliance                                                                             |
| 3. Minutes                               | → Read the Minutes of the Board meetings to identify the significant decisions made and their impact on the financial statements.                                                                   |
| 4. Evaluation of Internal Control System | → Obtain an understanding of Internal Control System and evaluate the Internal Control System to know about operating effectiveness.<br>→ This helps the auditor to plan his substantive procedures |
| 5. Correspondence                        | → Examine the certificates and other correspondences with the legal authorities to confirm exemptions etc. If any.                                                                                  |


### B. Audit of Receipts/ Incomes

 1. **Income From Fees** 
	→ Examine the list of students and fees criteria.
	→ Identify the rates of:
		☑ Tuition Fees
		☑ Admission Fees
		☑ Others Fees: Exam Fees, Extra Curricular Activities Etc.
	→ Cross check the sample of fees demanded and fees collected.
	→ Ensure that the amount received is properly accounted.
	→ For any discounts on fees, ensure that it is properly authorized.
	→ Cross check the copies of receipts issued and the cash/ bank account.
	→ Ensure that the fees income is properly booked in books of accounts.
	→ Ensure proper adjustment in accounts for the fees paid in advance.
	→ Confirm that fines for late payment or absence etc. have either been collected or remitted under proper authority.
	→ For Hostel Facility, examine the terms and conditions and vouch the income from students.  



 2. **Income from Donation and Grants** 
	→ Check the nature of Grant: Whether Specific or General
	→ Study the grant sanction letter to identify the terms and conditions of the grant.
	→ Ensure that these terms and conditions have been properly complied with.
	→ Check the accounting entries for the grant received or refunded.  


 3. **Rental Income** 
→ Sometimes the portion of building or asset acquired is sublet for rental income.
→ Study the rental agreement with the tenant.
→ Ensure that the rental income is properly accounted in books of accounts.
→ Examine the treatment for TDS deducted on rental income.
→ Check the bank/ cash account to confirm the rental receipts.  


  4. Income from Investments 
	→ Examine the minutes for the decision relating to investments.
	→ Ensure that the investment made is within the objective of the company.
	→ Inspect the securities in respect of investment held
	→ Vouch income from endowments and legacies, as well as interest and dividends from in investment  


### C. Audit of Payments/ Expenses

 1. **Administrative Expenses** 
For *day to day administrative expenses*, the auditor should check:
☑ Authorization
☑ Invoices
☑ Accounting

For *Scheduled expenses such as Salaries*, Rent etc, the auditor should check:
☑ Agreement (Rental/ Employee Contract)
☑ Terms of payment
☑ Accounting
☑ Tax-Implications (whether the tax has been properly deducted and deposited)
☑ Mode of Payment (cash/ cheque) *
☑ Acknowledgement by payee (receipt/ signed slip etc)

* The auditor has to cross check the Bank/ Cash Ledger to confirm the payment  


  2. **Expenses toward students** 
The expenses towards students may be in the nature of:
• Library Facility
• Prize and Scholarships
• Games and Sports etc.

The auditor has to:
☑ Check the policy of the institution for prize, scholarships and similar activities.
☑ Verify the amount spent on such activities with proper supporting (List of events, distribution etc)
☑ Examine the acknowledgment by the students on receipt of prize/ scholarship money.
☑ Examine the bills and invoices for the gift/ prize items bought.  |

### D. Audit of Assets

|                    |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Nature of Assets   | The assets of the educational institution may be in the nature of Furniture & Fixtures, Library, Laboratory, Computers, Building, Vehicle etc.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| General Procedures | ⇒ Obtain the list of assets owned by the entity.<br>⇒ Ensure that these assets are properly classified according to their nature.<br>⇒ Verify few assets physically.<br>⇒ For newly acquired assets, examine the minutes and invoices of the asset.<br>⇒ Verify whether the depreciation has been properly provided.<br>⇒ Obtain written representation regarding the ownership, existence and valuation of the assets.<br>⇒ Ensure that obsolete items are properly separated and the disposal is properly accounted. |



### E. Audit of Liabilities

| Nature of Liabilities | The Liabilities of the educational institutions are mainly in the nature of Student Deposits, Security Deposits (Library, Laboratory), loans from the financial institutions etc.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| General Procedu → Obtain the list of deposits from the students and identify the nature of such deposits.<br>→ For deposits outstanding for a long period, enquire with the management.<br>→ Confirm that caution money and other deposits paid by students on admission have been shown as liability in the balance sheet and not transferred to Profit and Loss account.<br>→ Ensure that the education tax payable is properly reflected.<br>→ Verify the calculation for education tax.   ax.   ax.   |


## 14.2 AUDIT OF HOTELS

→ Hotel business is related to hospitality industry. In a country like Nepal, Hotel business has contributed to inflow of foreign currency and worldwide recognition of Nepalese hospitality.<br/>
→ Hotel business may range from lodges to five stars. However the general business principles for entire range are somehow similar.

### A. Understanding the Entity and Planning Activities

|  1. AOA / MOA | Study the AOA and MOA of the Hotel to identify the objectives, powers and governance structure.  |
| --- | --- |
|  2. Internal Rules | Study the internal rules and regulations governing the hotel.  |
|  3. Minutes | Read the Minutes of the Board meetings to identify the significant decisions made and their impact on the financial statements. For eg: Investments, Purchase of assets etc.  |
|  4. Compliance | Ensure that the Hotel has taken permission from Nepal Rastra Bank for foreign currency transactions  |
|  5. Evaluation of Internal Control System | Obtain an understanding of Internal Control System and evaluate the operating effectiveness.  |
|  6. Accounting Policies | Obtain an understanding of accounting policies adopted by the hotel.  |
|  7. Industry Regulations | Obtain an understanding of hotel industry regulations and trends to identify the category of incomes, expenses, tax implications etc.  |



### B. Audit of Receipts/ Incomes

 1. **Income from Room Sales** 
	Study the tariff rates applicable to various categories of rooms such as:
	• Normal Rooms, Deluxe Rooms, Suites etc
	Study the guest register to identify occupancy ratio.
	• Ensure that the guests are billed at proper rates.
	For any discounts given, ensure that it was properly authorized.
	Check the arithmetical accuracy of bills accounted.
	**Mode of Receipt**
		• The Guests may pay in cash/ cheque, foreign currency or through credit cards.
		• The auditor has to ensure the compliance with foreign currency regulation of Nepal Rastra Bank
		• For Cash/ Cheque payments, examine the cash/ bank ledgers.  



2. **Income from Restaurants** 
	• Examine Kitchen Order Tickets (KOT’s) and cross verify with the copies of invoice.
	• Check cash ledger to verify the cash receipts.
	• Ensure that the discounts are properly authorized.
	• Check the internal controls over food stuff.  


3. **Commission Income** 
• Hotel may derive commission income for referring guests to Travel agencies, airlines etc.
• Auditor should check such commission agreements.
• Ensure that the commission income is properly accounted.  


  4. **Miscellaneous Income** 
	• Other Income of Hotel may be:
	• Income from events (party/ seminars), Gymnasium, Swimming Pool, Rent to Shopkeepers etc.
	• The auditor shall:
	• Obtain an understanding of the rates applicable
	• Check the copies of invoices and receipts
	• Ensure proper accounting and posting etc.  

 5. **Disposal of Assets** 
	• The hotel may discard various old assets such as furniture, carpets, vehicles etc.
	• The auditor shall ensure that:
	• the disposal is properly authorized
	• the income from disposal of such assets is properly accounted for.  



### C. Audit of Payments/Expenses


1. Purchase of Goods
	➔ The auditor should ensure whether:
	✓ The purchases are properly authorized
	✓ The purchases are supported by genuine invoices
	✓ The Purchases are properly classified  

 2. Salary and Wages 
	➔ Identify the criteria for payment to staffs
	➔ Check the category of labours i.e. permanent or casual
	➔ Check the attendance records and wages payment registers
	➔ Perform ARP to identify the variations if any.
	➔ Ensure that the Taxes have been properly deducted and deposited.
	➔ Examine the cash/ bank ledge to confirm the payments  


  3. Other Administrative Expenses 
	➔ Check whether the expenses are incurred for the business purpose.
	➔ Check the invoices for material expenses
	➔ Ensure that the expenses are recorded under proper headings.
	➔ Examine the invoices.
	➔ Cross check the cash/ bank ledger.  

 4. Commission Expenses 
	➔ Check the agreements entered into with the travel agencies
	➔ Ensure that the payment has been made as per the agreements
	➔ Ensure that the TDS has been properly accounted.
	➔ Verify whether the total commission expenses are properly charged to Profit and Loss account.  


  5. Capital Expenses 
	➔ Hotel may incur material expenses for expansion and renovation.
	➔ Study the minutes for the decision related to the expansion and renovation.
	➔ Vouch the bills and invoices related to such expenses
	➔ Ensure that all the material expenses are properly accounted
	➔ Check whether the expenses are properly capitalized  

### D. Assets

**Nature of Assets**
The Assets of hotel include building, structures, furniture, Generator, Kitchen Equipment. Stock, Vehicles, etc.


**General Procedures**
	→ The General steps for audit of assets include:
		✓ Ascertain the cost
		✓ Check authorization for new purchase and invoices
		✓ Ensure correctness of valuation
		✓ Conduct physical verification
		✓ Ensure that the asset has been properly depreciated
		✓ Ensure appropriate disclosures related to assets.  


**Special Attentions** 
	**Luxury Items**
		→ Hotels usually have luxury items which are highly priced and are much more prone to risk of misappropriation.
		→ Therefore the auditor has to check proper internal controls for such assets and verify their physical existence by comparing with the list of records maintained.
	**Stocks**
		→ The food and beverage stock of hotel is also readily tradable item.
		→ The auditor should ensure that all movements and transfer of such stocks is properly documented.
		→ The auditor should carry out tests to ensure that all such documentation is accurately processed
	**Foreign Exchange and Cash Balance**
		→ The hotel often has permission obtained for Nepal Rastra Bank for foreign currency transactions.
		→ Check the compliance with the requirement of Nepal Rastra Bank for foreign currency transactions.
